text:
# eventsourced-ai — agent notes

## Architecture map (for fast orientation)

Event-sourced: append-only event store ("AoL" stream, OCC appends), sessions are event
streams folded into state, read models are disposable projections.

- **Event store port**: `internal/ports/eventstore.go` (`Store.Append`); adapter
  `internal/adapters/eventstore/aol/store.go` (plus `drive.go`, `drive_mem.go`,
  `history.go`). Every successful `Append` canonicalizes events
  (`domain.Canonical`) and then notifies subscribers
  (`ports.AppendBroadcaster`/`SubscribeAppend`, `aol/observe.go`) — the hook
  the stream processor consumes. `internal/ports/stream.go` defines
  `EventBatch`/`AppendObserver`/`SessionReader`.
- **Stream processor** (2026-09-08 redesign): `internal/streamproc` — THE read
  seam. The orchestrator is the single writer AND consumer of the AOL store,
  so in-memory projections subscribe to the append bus instead of re-reading
  files. Key files: `engine.go` (wiring; `Attach` subscribes `SessionView` +
  `ToolLedger` + `ToolRoundView` BEFORE restoring so mid-restore batches dedupe
  by position; `NewRunner` subscribes each tailing runner to the bus — a runner
  built any other way never sees live appends), `sessionview.go` (`SessionView`,
  implements `ports.SessionReader` = `Session`/`Events`/`Window`; per-session
  slice + lazy `domain.Fold`; snapshot validated against the store head on
  first read, stale snapshot → one-time full replay), `toolledger.go`
  (`ToolLedger`, the `ports.ToolDispatchStore` — replaced coord.json; ONE
  `apply` path shared by bus and boot replay; checkpointed like the runners:
  the snapshot holds the outstanding requests + dispatch/lease marks at a
  global position, so a boot folds only the delta; a legacy jobs-only snapshot
  is still read as the fallback), `toolround.go` (`ToolRoundView`, checkpointed
  the same way — rounds + touched times at a position, delta replay;
  `snaps == nil` keeps the old full-replay behavior), `runner.go`
  (`Runner`: queue between bus and `Apply` on its own goroutine, wake-channel
  — no polling, global-position checkpoint anchor-validated at boot,
  per-drain checkpoint mark), `snapshot.go` (write-behind temp+rename into
  `<AOL dir>/projections/`; derived/disposable — losing one costs a replay).
  Consumers: `Loop.session/state/sessionEvents` (`internal/orchestrator/views.go`),
  `HTTP.Views` + `InstanceController.WithSessions` (both `ports.SessionReader`),
  tailing views instances/sessions/memory/digest in
  `internal/adapters/projection/memory` (SessionsView derives its rows from
  SessionView folds — it has no state machine of its own). The ONLY sanctioned
  direct reads of session streams are time-travel replays via
  `internal/orchestrator/replay.go` (`FoldAt`; serves `promptAt` +
  `contextReplay`) and the digest view; worker system streams
  (`Instance.StreamID()` = `<kind>:<id>`, e.g. `code:k8s-...`;
  `domain.IsWorkerStream` recognizes both that and the legacy
  `worker:<kind>:<id>` shape) are read directly by the instance controller.
- **Canonical pointer events**: `Append` normalizes via `domain.Canonical`
  (`internal/domain/registry.go`), so bus, stream files, and `Load` all
  deliver exactly ONE Go type per event (the decoders' pointer forms).
  Type-switch on pointers only — no more value+pointer double switches;
  `ports.ToolDispatch.Event`/`StaleToolRun.Event` are `*domain.ToolCallRequested`.
- **Orchestrator**: wired in `cmd/orchestrator/main.go`; core loop
  `internal/orchestrator/loop.go` (`runRound` ~:253, `HandleUserMessage`,
  `HandleToolCompletion` :296), driver `internal/orchestrator/drive.go`
  (`DriveSessions` :55, lease-based pump; the WAITING_TOOLS park re-verifies
  via `ToolRoundView` — `roundSettled`, fold fallback — and in pool mode with
  `TOOL_ROUND_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` set parks then waits on the round, re-claiming
  as the pump's next pass), HTTP+SSE API `internal/orchestrator/http.go`
  (route table :41-158) and `internal/orchestrator/sse.go` (`ActivityHandler` :20,
  `GET /api/sessions/:id/activity`).
- **Workers**: `internal/worker/instance.go` (`Announce/Ping/Stop` :58/:100/:135, each
  owns a system stream `worker:<kind>:<id>`); binaries `cmd/worker-code`,
  `cmd/worker-tools`, `cmd/worker-mcp`. Jobs arrive via RabbitMQ (`agent.tools` topic
  exchange, `ports.ToolJob` in `internal/ports/broker.go:15`, publishing in
  `internal/adapters/rabbitmq/rabbitmq.go:329`; results consumed by every orchestrator,
  only the session-owning instance applies them).
- **Worker liveness is memory-only** (2026-09-08): pongs do NOT append a durable
  `worker_instance_ping` — `InstanceController.handlePong` touches the
  controller lease and the registry read model via `ports.WorkerLease`
  (`InstanceView.TouchLastSeen`). Liveness is a NOW answer, not replayable
  history; worker streams keep only announce/stop (probe answering is
  idempotent via the controller's in-memory probe map). This also removed the
  pprof #1: per-pong full `Store.Load` replays of the worker stream (90% of
  orchestrator CPU). Worker-stream reads go through the in-memory projection
  (`InstanceController.workerEvents`); digest triggers read via
  `SessionReader` too (`DigestView.WithSessions`).
- **The registry retires pod generations, and event-less state is checkpointed**
  (2026-09-17). Two consequences of the memory-only design above, both of which
  grew with every deploy: `probeRound` probes every entry `ListInstances`
  returns, and a lease stop is not a durable append, so it only survived a
  restart through `InstanceView`'s snapshot. A Deployment gives every rollout's
  pods a fresh name, so the registry otherwise accumulated one entry per pod
  incarnation forever (measured on prod: 153 "alive" instances from 09-10
  onwards against 13 real workers, i.e. 1071 probe publishes in the 90s
  `GoneAfter` window, re-run on EVERY boot because the sweep's retirement had
  never been persisted). Now: `InstanceView.pruneSupersededLocked` drops a
  worker's older generations (`generationKey`/`podOwner` strip the k8s
  `<pod-template-hash>-<pod-suffix>` tail; a name without that shape — a locally
  started `k8s-mats-go-auth-main`, whose last segment is "main" — is its own
  owner) at announce time and again on `Restore`, so a restored zombie farm
  collapses instead of being re-probed; it never drops the newest generation of
  a worker, nor a predecessor still ponging (a rollout overlaps old and new
  pods), and `aol-gc` deletes the corresponding dead stream files off disk. And
  `ports.DirtyStateProjection` (`StateDirty`, cleared by `Snapshot`) lets the
  runner stage a checkpoint for state no event carried — `Runner.checkpointDirty`
  on `IdleCheckpoint` (10s) — so a sweep's retirement is durable seconds later
  instead of waiting for the next append to drain. Together: one sweep per dead
  generation, ever, and a registry bounded by live workers rather than by deploy
  count.
- **Session↔worker binding** (2026-09-06): a session routes by a pinned worker
  instance (`extra.worker` = instance id) plus the workspace folder on it
  (`extra.workspace` = checkout path — the primary routing + allowed_root
  claim). `extra.repo` is the optional fallback claim (remote#branch or path)
  and the provisioning identity `provision_worker` uses. Resolution lives
  in `resolveDispatchTarget` (`internal/orchestrator/dispatch.go`); strict
  dispatch fails a round whose binding resolves to no alive instance
  (`REPO_UNAVAILABLE`, the pin doubles as the revive hint).
  **Tag routing** (2026-09-10): `extra.tags` (comma-separated, set via the
  `tags` context key) matches against the Capabilities workers announce
  (superset semantics; `domain.TagsMatch`/`SessionTags`).Precedence: pin > tags > repo > plain global. `pickDispatchInstance` and
  `globalWorkerOffersTool` filter candidates by tags; a tags-only session is a
  strict claim and fails with `WORKER_TAGS_UNAVAILABLE` (`tagsUnavailableMessage`,
  hints via `strictTagAnnouncers` on the same repo_unavailable.v1 marker).
  When a resolved pin is wiped (the pinned worker does not announce the tool),
  the escape set is doubly constrained for a pin+tags session: only repo-less
  global workers announcing every session tag may serve the call
  (`pickGlobalDispatchInstance`, never another repo worker's tree), and the
  strict failure names the pin (instance id + workspace) plus the tags so a
  replacement worker knows what to announce.
  A specialized worker (e.g. future `cmd/worker-esp`) is just a new kind
  announcing `WORKER_CAPABILITIES` + tool specs — no core changes. The k8s controller
  clones repos onto workers (`internal/adapters/k8s/controller.go`); a locally
  started worker-code announces its own checkouts via `RepoRoots()` — either
  way the folder is what sessions bind to. UI: session dialog + workspace
  picker in `web/src` (`repoHelpers.bindingLabel`).
- **Dev-port expose (2026-09-10)**: a worker pod port is published behind a
  Service + Ingress on a wildcard parent domain (`*.preview.k6n.net` default;
  `PREVIEW_DOMAIN`/`PREVIEW_INGRESS_CLASS`/`PREVIEW_CLUSTER_ISSUER` env, wired
  into `ControllerOptions`). Host = `<token>.<domain>` where `<token>` is a
  short lowercase-base36 FNV-1a hash of the instance id + port (stable across
  calls); the port is always served at `/`, and re-exposing an already-exposed
  port returns the recorded host untouched (legacy long hosts included). The
  wildcard DNS record must point at the nginx ingress; the wildcard TLS secret
  (`preview-k6n-net-wildcard-tls`) covers every host, so there is no per-host
  cert wait. Entry points: the `repo.instance.expose`/`repo.instance.unexpose`
  builtins (instance_id defaults to the session's pinned worker `extra.worker`
  when omitted) and `POST /api/controller/instances/expose|unexpose`
  (authorized per worker+repo like every instance op); the Service/Ingress
  carry `eventsourced.ai/instance-id` labels so `ListInstances` attaches
  `ManagedInstance.Exposed` for the UI and `StopInstance` tears them down.
- **Web fetch/search worker** (2026-09-10): `cmd/worker-web` announces a `web`
  instance serving `web_fetch` (HTTP GET first; CDP fallback via chromedp
  against `CDP_ENDPOINT` — default headless-shell `10.10.3.27:9222`, k8s uses
  `http://headless-shell-service.dev.svc:9222`) and `web_search` against the
  SearXNG instance in namespace `search` (`SEARXNG_URL`, in-cluster
  `http://searxng.search.svc.cluster.local:8080`; public `https://search.k6n.net`
  serves `format=json` too). `websearch.Searcher` is the swappable-backend
  interface (Noop with a clear error when SEARXNG_URL is unset). Pipeline in
  `internal/adapters/webfetch` (fetch.go fallback heuristics incl. bot-wall
  markers, cdp.go shared remote allocator + per-tab fetches, sanitize.go
  x/net/html → text with a readability-lite density heuristic) +
  `internal/adapters/websearch`. No store, no repos — pure network egress,
  freely scalable; image `Dockerfile.worker-web` (distroless), manifest
  `deploy/k8s/worker-web.yaml`. CLI testing without RabbitMQ: `cmd/webfetch`
  (`get|search|doctor`; env `CDP_ENDPOINT`/`SEARXNG_URL`; flags may precede or
  follow the positional URL/query).
- **Context7 + modern-web guidance** (2026-09-10): the same `web` instance
  also serves `context7_search`/`context7_docs` (up-to-date third-party
  library docs; canonical libraryId e.g. `/reactjs/react.dev` then
  topic lookup) and `modern_web_search`/`modern_web_guide`/`modern_web_list`
  (curated best-practice guides for modern CSS/HTML APIs/performance/a11y;
  ranked ids then raw-Markdown fetch, plus a full catalog with client-side
  category filter), all backed by the self-hosted doc-sources API
  (`DOC_SOURCES_URL`, in-cluster
  `http://doc-sources.search.svc.cluster.local:3000`, public
  `https://search.k6n.net` — the same `search` namespace/domain as SearXNG).
  `docsources.DocSources` is the swappable-backend interface (Noop with a
  clear error when DOC_SOURCES_URL is unset), implemented by
  `internal/adapters/docsources` (search JSON + raw-Markdown fetches; guide
  content injects straight into LLM context). CLI testing without RabbitMQ:
  `cmd/webfetch` `context7|context7docs|mweb|mwebguide|mweblist` (env
  `DOC_SOURCES_URL`), plus a doc-sources probe in `doctor`.
- **MCP workers (2026-09-13)**: `cmd/worker-mcp` serves exactly ONE MCP server
  per process, selected by `MCP_SERVER_CONFIG` + `MCP_SERVER_NAME`
  (claude-desktop-style file, parsed by `mcp.LoadServer` in
  `internal/adapters/mcp` — per-entry `url`+`headers` or stdio
  `command`/`args`/`env`), or `MCP_SERVER_URL`/`MCP_SERVER_HEADERS`, or a
  stdio `MCP_SERVER_COMMAND`. Each config entry carries `auth`
  (`none|static|oauth|per_user`; default static when headers present),
  optional `category` (default `MCP_CATEGORY`=`mcp`), and `tools.allow`/`deny`
  filters that override `MCP_INCLUDE_TOOLS`/`MCP_EXCLUDE_TOOLS`
  (`mcp.Filter` — allowlist first, then denylist; bare names or
  `category.name` keys). `${VAR}` references in header/env values resolve from
  the process environment at load time (unset → fatal at boot), so tokens live
  in Secrets and never in the config file. Auth modes: `static` shares one
  credential per worker and skips the per-user dispatch grant
  (`Loop.mcpStaticAuth`, dispatch.go mcp gate); `oauth` is the existing device
  flow; `per_user` resolves a pre-provisioned per-user token
  (`mcpoauth.UserFileStore.StaticTokenForSubject`,
  `<sha256(subject)>.static.json` under `MCP_USER_TOKENS_DIR`, fallback to
  shared headers) and caches one client per `origin_subject` — no
  single-user binding. Workers announce their mode (`WorkerAnnounced.AuthMode`
  → `ports.WorkerInstance.AuthMode` → `InstanceView`; empty = legacy
  behavior). Instantiation mirrors code workers:
  `provision_worker`/`repo.instance.start`/`POST /api/controller/instances/start`
  accept `kind: mcp` + `mcp_server` (+ optional `mcp_secret`),
  `k8s.Controller.startMCPInstance` renders the pod (no checkout, mounts the
  `eventsourced-mcp-config` ConfigMap at /config, envFrom's the token Secret,
  emptyDir for `MCP_AUTH_STATE_DIR`/`MCP_USER_TOKENS_DIR`, image
  `Dockerfile.worker-mcp` with `-tags web_worker`), and
  `deploy/k8s/worker-mcp.yaml` is the static always-on variant (applied
  manually — it owns the ConfigMap; never add it to `deploy-all`).
  `announcedInstanceID`/`bareInstanceID` have kind-aware twins
  (`kindAnnouncedInstanceID` etc.) and ManagedInstance.Repo is empty for mcp.
  `GET /api/controller/mcp/servers` lists the configured entries secret-free
  (`mcp.ListServers`; ConfigMap in-cluster, `MCP_SERVER_CONFIG` file in dev)
  for the sidebar's MCP pane (`SidebarMCPWorkers`, manage tab → MCP Workers
  sub-toggle; the code-worker pane filters repo-less deployments out).
- **Shared user browser (2026-09-14)**: `cmd/worker-browser` is the gateway for
  the Chrome extension in `browser-extension/` (loaded unpacked; `icon.svg` is
  the raster source). The extension dials the worker's WebSocket, sends a
  `hello` (token/protocol/session), then serves `request` frames; the worker
  validates the hello (`helloRejectReason`) and pings every 15s so Chrome does
  not reap the MV3 service worker. Frames live in `internal/browserbridge`
  (`Frame`); `Arguments` is a JSON **string** on the wire — the extension parses
  the whole frame first, so an inline object arrived as a JS object and its own
  `JSON.parse` threw `"[object Object]" is not valid JSON`, which broke every
  `user_browser.*` call. Tools: `user_browser.open/action/screenshot/close` plus
  `user_browser.macro`; the `action` enum (reload/back/forward/inspect/text/
  query/evaluate/click/type/press/select/hover/scroll/wait_for/console) is
  implemented in the extension, so a new action is a worker-spec + extension
  change with no orchestrator change. Two worlds matter: console capture and
  `evaluate` run in the page's MAIN world (only there is the real `console`/
  page globals reachable), everything else in the isolated world (chrome.*
  available); hooks are re-installed on navigation. Macros record→replay the
  user's own gestures with password/payment fields redacted at capture
  (`values[selector]` required to replay them). Agent-callable tab switching is
  deliberately absent — one explicitly shared tab is the contract. Every call is
  **bounded at both ends** (2026-09-14): the extension gives each call its own
  budget (`callTimeout` — the call's own `timeout_ms` plus margin for `wait_for`,
  120s for macro replay, 30s otherwise) and answers with an actionable error
  rather than leaving the request unanswered, while `cmd/worker-browser` bounds
  its wait through `browserCallBudget` (deliberately a few seconds wider, so the
  extension's specific error normally wins the race and that bound only fires
  when the extension is wedged). Both halves are needed because a call that never
  settles used to hold the worker's job consumer (observed: `captureVisibleTab`
  while the user had switched away from the shared tab) for the whole 5-minute job
  timeout, so every later call on that worker failed as `NOT_STARTED` — a browser
  bug presenting as unrelated tools breaking. That consumer now runs **per-session
  lanes** (`jobLanes` in `internal/adapters/rabbitmq`, 2026-09-14): one session's
  jobs stay strictly in arrival order — the orchestrator publishes a round's tool
  calls back-to-back and models emit order-dependent batches (`writefile` then
  `bash`), and one tab cannot run two actions at once — while different sessions
  run concurrently up to `Client.JobConcurrency` (`WORKER_JOB_CONCURRENCY`, default
  4, 1 = strictly serial). The same number is the consumer's prefetch, so a crash
  redelivers at most that many, and the read loop hands work to a lane instead of
  running it, so no session can block the delivery of another's.
  `Bridge.failPending` closes the other half: a socket that goes away
  (killed MV3 worker, closed tab, reconnect) fails its in-flight calls at once
  instead of waiting out the caller's context. `screenshot` activates the shared
  tab first, because `captureVisibleTab` captures the window's *active* tab — so
  a backgrounded share used to capture a different page, or never settle at all —
  and never ships the raw viewport PNG: the extension rescales it to
  `SCREENSHOT_MAX_SIDE` (1500) and re-encodes as JPEG (`SCREENSHOT_QUALITY` 72)
  before the bytes leave the browser. That has to happen client-side because
  `materializeArtifacts` only strips `data_base64` out of the *event* while
  `providerMessages` re-attaches the full image to every LLM message that
  carries it, so the size is paid on each round (a 1920x1080 capture: 3.7 MB
  PNG / ~5 MB base64 vs ~107 KB as JPEG). Source stays PNG so the JPEG pass is
  the only lossy generation; `max_side`/`quality` per call override the
  defaults, the result carries `width`/`height` (the returned image's real
  dimensions, as `browser.screenshot` in cmd/worker-web does) plus `scaled`, and
  an unavailable/fruitless resize falls back to the original bytes with a
  `resize_error` instead of losing the capture. The
  dashboard's browser pane reads the extension's saved macros through
  `GET /api/sessions/{id}/browser/macros` (`browsermacros.go` → the
  `browser_macros` worker RPC op → the extension WebSocket): a live relay, since
  the macro store is extension-local, so an unbound session is a 409 and an
  offline extension a 502 rather than an empty list. It asks for
  `{action:list,summary:true}` — names and step counts, never the steps. The same
  pane lists the `user_browser.action` verbs, parsed from the announced spec
  (`parameters.properties.action.enum`) with no extra endpoint.
- **Event types**: `internal/domain/events.go` (constants :73-105). Fold:
  `internal/domain/context.go` / `session.go`; projections
  `internal/adapters/projection`. LLM digesting + RAG memory sync run as
  in-process projections in `cmd/orchestrator` (the old standalone
  `cmd/projector` is gone), so the store dir keeps exactly ONE writer
  process — in batched mode (`AOL_FLUSH_MS>0`) a second writer truncates
  stream files back to its own cursor and corrupts them (the NFS NUL-byte
  incident of 2026-09-06). The AOL reader skips corrupt lines (logged) and a
  batched store claims `writer.lock` so a second batched opener fails at
  boot. Workers never touch the store (broker only), so the append bus needs
  no cross-process notification.
- **Persisted read index (default on; 2026-09-17)**: `aol.Open` used to
  re-read and JSON-parse every line of every stream file on every boot — the
  last unbounded startup cost, untouched by the projection checkpoints. It now
  restores that index instead: `<AOL>/index.json` is a JSON header (format/
  parser versions, checksum, one entry per stream) plus a varint row blob, and
  every stream is reconciled against the extent recorded with it (`size == next`
  → install with no stream read at all; larger → tail-read what was appended
  while down; smaller/absent/undecodable → re-scan that ONE file). On the
  PRODUCTION store (252 streams, 34 869 events) that is 169.9 MB of streams →
  a 2.74 MB index (1.6% of them) and a 1.0 s boot → 24–32 ms: 32–42x, verified
  row-for-row identical to a full scan of the same files. Rows are binary
  precisely because the JSON-row first cut measured at only 1.2x — decoding the
  JSON alone cost as much as parsing the streams. It is derived data, so every
  failure degrades to the full scan and the boot decision is logged every time;
  `AOL_INDEX=0` disables, `AOL_REINDEX=1` forces one rebuild, and `index.lock`
  names the single writer so a secondary opener reads but never rewrites. Rows
  are written when the index is built, on `Close`, and mid-run only once the
  drift crosses `max(512, covered/4)` — keeping index write volume O(stream
  bytes) instead of O(bytes × uptime / interval). A derivation change may only
  land WITH a version bump (`indexParserVersion` rows / `indexFormatVersion`
  layout): the mismatch discards the file for one full scan, and
  `TestReadIndexEncodingIsPinnedToItsVersion` pins the encoded bytes so a change
  cannot slip through unnoticed. Still O(history) in index BYTES and in the
  `byPos` array, both materialized at boot regardless — making that lazy is
  Layer 2 of `docs/plan_aol_index_persistence.md`. The aol package's test
  helpers open with the index ON (the production shape); `openPlain` /
  `WithReadIndex(false)` is the full-scan path.
- **`indexRow` is the one row derivation (2026-09-17)**: persisting the index
  made load-bearing a drift that used to look harmless. The two append paths in
  `store.go` built their own `posEntry` and omitted `at`, so `occurred_at` was
  EMPTY for every event appended since the last restart — the column the
  dashboard's history search displays and matches on — while a full scan
  backfilled it from the file. An index written in such a process would have
  restored the empty value for good. `indexRow` is now the single derivation
  shared by `parseLines` and both append paths, pinned by
  `TestAppendedRowsMatchParsedRows`, and it landed with `indexParserVersion=2`
  so a pre-fix index is discarded rather than trusted.
- **Digest settle flush (2026-09-14)**: the digest projection
  (`internal/adapters/projection/memory/digest.go`) has TWO triggers. Its round
  cadence (`Apply` on `agent_iteration_started`) still needs COMPACTION_ROUNDS new
  rounds, but the session driver now also calls `Loop.flushDigest` from the settle
  path in `drive.go` — where `session.idle` triggers already fire — so a session
  that rests before reaching the cadence still produces a summary and its promoted
  memories. `Flush` only queues (bounded, deduped by session); one worker drains it
  serially (`StartFlushWorker`, wired in `cmd/orchestrator/main.go` only when
  `COMPACTION_ENABLED`, via the `ports.DigestFlusher` port and `Loop.SetDigest`),
  and a per-session mutex serializes the two paths so a window can never be folded
  twice. The settle window ignores the round gate and, for a session SHORTER than
  COMPACTION_KEEP_TAIL_ROUNDS, folds the whole session (there is no verbatim tail
  worth protecting yet; long sessions keep their tail exactly as the cadence path
  leaves it). Nothing here reaches the model's prompt implicitly: the request
  budget is size-driven (`CompactionUseFraction` of the window), so a
  `session_compacted` anchor only replaces history near the model's maximum
  context — or when the user explicitly asks (`compaction_requested.v1`) — and
  the flush is additive to RAG. The one consumer that must NOT treat the anchor
  as history is `Fork`; see the next bullet.
- **Circuit forms and decisions (2026-09-19)**: `compaction_profile: "circuit"`
  turns a session into a Circuit-method INITIATIVE, and that one property is the
  only gate (`domain.IsCircuitSession`) — it selects the circuit historian prompt
  AND offers the `circuit.*` builtins. Two events carry the Forma (Shape) and
  Förvalta (Operate) views: `circuit_form_recorded.v1` (last-write-wins per form
  key, partial updates merge, the completeness verdict stored ON the event as a
  fact rather than recomputed on read) and `circuit_decision_recorded.v1` (an
  append-only hash chain verified in STREAM order, never by `at`). Three writers,
  one shape, distinguished only by `source`: the `circuit.record_form` /
  `circuit.record_decision` builtins (`internal/orchestrator/circuit.go`, the
  primary path), the compaction historian's new `forms`/`decisions` keys
  (`digestSystemPromptCircuit`, the safety net — it is an inference over a
  transcript and is forbidden from guessing), and eventually the UI. Every
  recording also dispatches the rendered markdown into the initiative's repo via
  `RequestSpecCommit`, because the repo copy — not the UI — is what an auditor
  reads. The rules are pure functions in `internal/domain/circuit.go`
  (completeness, the closed resource/decision enums, cost derived from the
  manifest and never stored, the four-eyes separation policy as DATA), so the
  tool, the compactor and a replay cannot disagree. Hashes, the actor's identity
  and the self-approval flag are all computed by the orchestrator and structurally
  unreachable from the model — a control the subject can set is not a control.
  `ports.HookInput` gained `actor` + `circuit` blocks so a policy hook decides
  against facts the orchestrator folded rather than reading the store itself. The
  read side is `GET /api/sessions/:id/circuit` (one fold: spec, the gate's named
  missing items, derived cost, the chain + its verdict, the per-recording history,
  the Q&A loop, and the state/phase replayed from the chain) plus
  `/circuit/doc?form=` for one form's repo markdown. The human write path
  (`PUT .../circuit/forms/{form}`, `POST .../circuit/decisions`) calls the SAME

- **Forks seed by prefix identity (2026-09-14)**: `Fork` asks ONE question —
  would the child's first request send the prompt prefix the parent's provider
  already cached? — and that decides the seed. **Yes**: a `context_imported`
  provenance header (source session, head, lane — **no** summary, so it renders
  nothing, see `context.go`) plus the parent's message-relevant events verbatim,
  so the child continues the parent's exact prefix on a cache hit. **No**: the
  child seeds from the parent's newest `session_compacted` (summary + the events
  after `covers_version`), trading fidelity for a guaranteed saving — a cold
  re-read of the whole history is the cost this avoids. The answer comes from
  `PrefixKey` (`internal/orchestrator/prefix.go`): provider, model, system
  prompt, tool surface and render policy — everything a provider folds into a
  cached prefix, deliberately excluding the history itself. Each round records
  its key on `AgentIterationStarted.PrefixKey`, and the fork recomputes the
  child's through the same `prefixKeyFor` builder, so a registry / models.json /
  skill / budget change since the parent's round reads as a mismatch, and a lane
  change (different model) is one by construction. The render policy digests only
  the STABLE budget inputs (tool-result cap, pruning knobs, the model's window,
  `compaction_use_fraction`); the DERIVED char budgets (`MaxTotalChars`, and the
  size line `UseCompactionAboveChars`) are excluded because they are the window
  scaled by the session's MEASURED chars-per-token — the fork recomputes with the
  usage as it is now while the parent's round recorded the usage it had then, so
  including either would report "cold" on nearly every fork
  (`TestRenderPolicyIgnoresTheMeasuredSizeThreshold`). A cache older than
  `prefixCacheTTL` (5 min) is a mismatch too. A stream with NO recorded key
  (written before this existed) keeps the verbatim history: an unproven cache is
  no reason to hand a child a summary of its own parent. `SessionForked`
  `.VerbatimSeed` records which path ran, and `PrefixKey` is stored as a hash so
  no prompt text ever reaches an event or a log. On the verbatim path the seed is
  a genuine PREFIX COPY: copied events keep the parent's own VERSION numbers and
  the provenance header goes LAST, after what it describes. That matters because
  rendered text embeds a version wherever it tells the model how to re-read a
  truncated payload (`truncMarker`) or names a pruned call — renumbering shifted
  every one of those by the header's slot and broke byte-identity exactly for the
  sessions worth caching (`TestForkChildPromptIsByteIdenticalToTheParent`). `restampEvent`
  rewrites any event through the store's own payload codec (no per-type switch), so
  every event type copies. `forkSkip` is the exception list, and a mid-seed
  omission is expensive because it consumes the version the copied prefix needs
  (the store requires contiguity from 1), which shifts every later event and
  breaks the prefix from that point on. Only two exceptions remain:
  `session_branched` (its fold EXCISES a version range, so in a renumbered child
  it would cut real history) and `session_stopped` POSITIONALLY — a trailing stop
  with no routed message is dropped, because the child would stay in the sticky
  STOPPED status with nothing to lift it and dropping the last event shifts
  nothing. Everywhere else a stop is copied: since 2026-09-14 halting is
  flow-only (`domain.SessionStopped` is not a `ContextContributor` and renders no
  prompt text — it controls which rounds run, never what the model is sent), so
  copying it changes no token of the request and the child is lifted exactly as
  the parent was, by the user message that follows
  (`TestForkChildPromptIsByteIdenticalAfterAStopAndResume`). The parent's own
  provenance — its `session_forked` markers and its `context_imported` header —
  is copied too, which closed the two flows that used to shift: forking a FORK
  (the child's own header sits mid-seed once it has run a round) and forking a
  session that was already forked FROM (its marker sits mid-seed). Neither is the
  child's data — a marker renders nothing and has no fold case, and a header
  renders a note only when it carries a summary, in which case that note IS part
  of the parent's prompt, so copying is required for the prefix to match. The
  child's own header goes last and is its real origin, and the two readers that
  used to assume "one header, one marker set" filter instead: `useForkTree` takes
  the LAST header as the origin and only counts a marker whose child is actually
  named under this session (`<parent>/fork/<id>`), or a sibling the parent forked
  would render as this session's child. Still open: a BRANCHED parent is
  unalignable by construction — its active branch has a version hole where the
  abandoned range was, so its seed cannot keep the parent's versions. The cold
  path still copies the parent's newest
  `session_context_updated` (behavior snapshot: pinned prompt + capability-policy
  enforcement, with `lane` cleared so the fork's own lane wins) — a behavior pin,
  not a cache artifact, so a child of a skilled parent never runs a looser toolset.

  `SidebarInstances` (`useInstanceManager` + `InstanceCard` + `ManualStartForm`
  + `AvailableReposPanel`), `InstancesView` (the wide cluster view, mounted as
  the `instances` sub-tab of the admin `DebugView` in `PageTabs` — pure layout
  over `useInstanceManager`, so instances have ONE data path) and the
  simple-mode `PreviewPanel` (same expose pieces, `size="md"` + plain labels,
  `ExposedPortRow` without `onUnexpose` — a business owner may open the preview,
  not take it down). Superseded dead chrome is gone (`WorkspaceSidebar` —
  `WorkspaceView` renders the same four panels; `SidebarDebugSnapshot` + its
  `web/src/hooks/useControllerDebug.ts` adapter — the admin debug panel
  replaced it, so `components/instances`' `useControllerDebug` is the only
  controller-debug fetch). Still parked: `ContextReplayView` (behind a
  commented-out `replay` tab). `SessionBindingChip` is now wired into
  `SessionBar`, right after the session id: it answers "which project is this
  session working on?" from the caches the stream already invalidates (the
  overview for live workers + the session-state snapshot per domain burst), so
  it polls nothing; its `simple` prop swaps the machine rows (serving instance
  id, workspace, checkout path, head, tags, restricted) for just the project
  and branch, keeping the live/amber state and the "no alive worker" warning.
  **Viewer-aware values** follow the simple-mode rework
  (`app-context.simpleMode` + `useSimpleMode()` in `components/chat/useIsAdmin`):
  containers read it, leaf pieces take a prop, and operator-only surfaces read
  nothing because the host gates them — `components/instances` is mounted behind
  `SidebarContent`'s `canManage` (`isAdmin && !simpleMode`), so it stays pure.
  `WorkerFileViewer` splits the difference: its intel strip (fresh parse,
  Symbols/Callers) defaults to `!simpleMode` (`showIntel` overrides, and
  `useFileIntel({enabled:false})` then issues no parse request), while its code
  surface, pager and code-focus strip stay for every viewer. `useSimpleModeOptional`/
  `useAppContextOptional` exist so a package component embedded without the app
  shell reads the defaults instead of throwing.
- **Search engine** (merged into this repo as a single module; was the sibling
  `codesearch` repo): embeddable facade `pkg/searcher` (Open/Close, `Search`,
  `Outline`, `Overview`, `Runtime`, `Refresh`), internals `internal/{index,store,
  ast,hybrid,embed,walk,text,query,symrank,runtimegraph,…}`, CLI binaries
  `cmd/cs`, `cmd/cs-mcp`, `cmd/benchmark`. Keep `internal/types` JSON field
  names stable — they are the agent-facing contract. The engine's own tests
  (incl. the CLI suite in `cmd/cs/cli`) run in this repo's `go test ./...`;
  `TestDoctorLiveOrMissingOutput` only asserts the missing-model health
  verdict when no embedder has been warmed in the process yet (any earlier
  test's background load makes the simulation unreliable).

- **Codesearch freshness + CLI (`cs`)** (2026-09-14): the graph tools
  (code_tree/code_context/code_callers/code_related/code_outline) never
  answer from a silently stale index. `internal/service/freshen.go`
  (`OpenFreshStore`, on the query path): small drift (≤32 changed/unindexed
  files) re-indexes inline before answering — Index is incremental and
  ctx-cancellable; large drift (fresh checkout, big rebase) starts ONE
  single-flight background pass and `Tree` answers from its live AST walk
  instead of stale symbols (the failure that used to show up as "matches no
  symbol" in 0ms). Complements, not replaces, the worker's existing layers:
  edit-triggered auto-index queue, `WarmIndexes`/`MaintainIndexes`
  (WORKER_INDEX_ON_START / WORKER_INDEX_WATCH_SECONDS), and
  `CODESEARCH_AUTO_INDEX=off` disables the request-path repair for
  watch-mode deployments. The `cs` binary now ships in the worker image —
  escape hatch, not the primary interface: the tools wrap the same engine
  with budgets, truncation and UI payloads, so prefer them; `cs` covers what
  they don't (`dead|hot|similar|top|stats`, `-json` scripting) plus manual
  `cs index` / `cs index --watch` upkeep.

- **ACP-backed subagent (2026-09-17)**: one extra `task.spawn` kind, `acp`
  (`internal/orchestrator/subtask.go`), whose "brain" is an external
  ACP-compatible agent binary instead of our own round loop — and it is a tool
  call, not a new loop: the child's profile is `SkipInline` (NO inline tools at
  all) plus the broker carve-out that offers exactly `acp.run`, announced by
  the code worker when `WORKER_ACP_AGENT_CMD` is set (`ACP_RUN_TIMEOUT`,
  default 10m; empty disables it, so a fleet without an agent binary is
  unchanged). The value is whitespace-split and exec'd directly — NOT run
  through a shell — and must name an executable present in the worker image;
  `docs/manual-code-worker.md` carries the working per-agent commands
  (`npx @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp`, `npx @google/gemini-cli --acp`,
  `goose acp`, …) and the credential caveat (the agent inherits the worker's
  env, and a provisioned worker pod receives no Secret keys).
  `internal/adapters/tools/acp` is the client: newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0
  over stdio, `initialize` → `session/new` → one `session/prompt`,
  with `fs/*`, `terminal/*` and `session/request_permission` served inbound on
  their own goroutines (an agent may call `terminal/wait_for_exit` mid-turn).
  Files stay inside `Manager.WorkdirFor(session)`; terminals go through
  `Manager.ExecArgs` (NOT `SpawnProcess`, which skips the policy engine) so an
  ACP shell command is assessed exactly like a `bash` call, and permission is
  auto-decided worker-side (read-only rejects mutating kinds) — no approval
  round-trip, per the plan's deferral. See §5b of `docs/plan_acp_subagent.md`
  for the accepted streaming design:
  `session/update` is accumulated into an in-memory transcript AND, since
  2026-09-17, coalesced into ephemeral progress — a `progressBatcher`
  (700 ms / 600 chars, boundary updates pass straight through) turns the
  agent's per-token chunks into a handful of `ports.WorkerActivity` items per
  turn, published on the `worker.activity` broker key (a FOURTH instance side
  channel, next to `worker.policy`) and republished by
  `InstanceController.handleActivity` on the feed the dashboard already has
  (`web/src/components/ActivityDrawer.tsx`) — under a detached, 5s-bounded
  context, so the final flush lands after the job context dies and a lost
  feed line is never a tool failure. Nothing about it is a `domain.Event`:
  the fold/registry/replay/compaction path is untouched, so the child stream
  keeps exactly the shape every subtask produces,
  `session_created → user_message_received → tool_call_requested(acp.run) →
  tool_call_completed → agent_message_completed`, and the exact-sequence test
  asserts it *unfiltered*. The result is `{answer, stop_reason, tool_calls}`
  and `SpawnSubtask`/`task.status`/the parent's result delivery are reused
  unchanged. Two bends are worth naming: `round.go` filters the `acp`
  category out of every ordinary session's offer (3 lines in `availableTools`,
  beside the pre-existing `gitopsCategory` skip — it changes the tool MENU,
  not how a round runs), and `dispatch.go` refuses a *guessed* `acp.run` by
  name with `UNKNOWN_TOOL`, because offer-filtering alone is not enforcement
  (dispatch has no "was this offered?" check, and unlike an ordinary unknown
  tool a code worker would happily fulfill the call). The budget is 4, not the
  literal 2: the wrap-up nudge fires two rounds before the cap, and at 3 it
  would land on the relay round itself. Deliberately not done: interactive
  approval, ACP-side token accounting, and lane routing for the external
  agent (see `docs/plan_acp_subagent.md` §5).

Build/test from the repo root with the usual Go toolchain:

```sh
go build ./...
go test ./...
```

## Skills and modes (2026-09-13, collapsed to ONE concept 2026-09-17): behavior = skill

A session's BEHAVIOR is one concept: a skill id. `internal/skills` is the declarative skill
loader (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter from `SKILLS_DIRS`, SHA-256 digests, immutable
registry). The six chat modes (`domain.ModeList`: exploration/poc/plan/task/feature/mob;
"normal" = no selection) are EMBEDDED BUILT-IN SKILLS: `skills.LoadDirs` seeds them first, a
dir skill shadowing a built-in id is a startup error, and `Loop.skillRegistry()` falls back to
the built-ins when no registry is wired.

One table, one key, one slot, one policy:

- **One table** — `internal/domain/modes.go` defines each mode ONCE (`modeDefs`, a `modeDef`
  with banner/label/icon/description/prompt/grant/deny). Label, icon, description and the
  capability pair used to live in eight parallel maps a new mode had to remember to join;
  `ModeSkillFor` projects the table into `skills.Builtin` and `ModePrompt` reads the same entry.
- **One write key** — `SessionContextUpdate` has no `Mode`: the write path records `skill`,
  period (`POST /sessions` and `/context` bodies too; the frontend's one helper is
  `behaviorContextUpdate`). The `mode` field on `SessionCreated`/`SessionContextUpdated` is
  LEGACY and read-only, kept solely so a pre-unification stream still decodes. Validation is one
  check — the registry `Has(id)` — so an unknown behavior is a 400 (`errInvalidContextSkill`) and
  there is no second "unknown mode" error to drift.
- **One slot** — `Loop.systemPrompt`/`behaviorPrompt` (in `subtask.go`, shared by the subtask
  and general branches so a child and its parent answer the same way) composes the skill
  snapshot, falls back to the live registry, then to an explicit `[SKILL UNAVAILABLE]` note, and
  renders `domain.ModePrompt` ONLY for a legacy-mode stream (`banner + body`, byte-identical, so
  an old session's fork prefix key stays stable). `ApplySessionContext` deletes the legacy
  `mode` extra whenever a skill is set, so the two can never compose together — the rule lives
  on the fold, not in callers.
- **One reader** — `domain.SessionBehaviorID(meta)` is the only place the skill→mode fallback
  lives; the trigger matcher (`triggerBehavior`), the mob approval guard and the summarizer all
  call it. Reading `extra["mode"]` alone was a live bug: a rule scoped to `feature` saw a
  session whose behavior arrived as a skill as `normal`. The client twin is
  `sessionBehaviorID(extra)` (`packages/ui/src/components/chat/behavior`), used by `ChatView`,
  the two session sidebars and the wizard picker — the same bug in the UI would have hidden the
  mob badge and the mob room for every mob session created after the collapse (they are written
  as `skill: mob` now, not `mode: mob`).
- **One policy** — capabilities only. A mode/skill LINKS a tool family with
  `grant_capabilities`/`deny_capabilities`; `allow_tools`/`deny_tools` are GONE from the model,
  the event snapshot (`BehaviorSnapshot.SkillGrantCapabilities`/`SkillDenyCapabilities`) and the
  spawn path, and enforcement is `filterSkillTools` (offer) + `skillToolCallPolicy` (dispatch)
  judging each tool by its declared `required_capabilities` — so exploration's read-only contract
  is a `filesystem.write` deny, not a list of tool names. `GET /api/skills` lists built-ins +
  dir skills; the web Behavior picker is one list. Skill `model_lane`/`max_rounds`/`requires` are
  declared but NOT yet consumed by the loop.

**One picker, with a face** (2026-09-17): because the modes ARE skills, any surface that
offered a mode row next to a skill list offered the same ids twice — and the two could
disagree (an explicit `skill` beats `mode` in `effectiveSkillID`, so a chip you clicked could
lose to a select you forgot). The wizard was the last one: `composeDraft` now holds ONE
`behavior` id, and the mode/skill wire split happens once, at create time, through
`behaviorContextUpdate` (`web/src/components/wizard/WizardComposeStep.tsx`; the composer's
`handleSelectBehavior` uses the same helper). A skill also carries `label` (the chip
caption, falling back to the id) and `icon` (an icon NAME — the registry is data and ships no
React component; the client maps the name in `components/chat/skillVisuals`), so chips and the
Behavior picker's rows read as names with icons instead of raw ids with a wand. Both fields are
deliberately OUTSIDE the digest's canonical form: a caption or icon swap must not read as a
contract change to a session that pinned the skill, nor as a provider-prefix mismatch to a fork
(`TestPresentationFieldsStayOutOfTheDigest`). Built-ins carry both from their `modeDefs` entry,
their descriptions carry no "Built-in: " prefix (since the unification there is no tier to
announce), and the shipped `skills/*.md` declare both. Selecting one shows `SkillCapabilities` under the chips: the
description for everyone, the granted/denied capabilities and tool exceptions only when
`!simpleMode` — capabilities rendered in plain words with the raw key beside them, because the
key alone names a privilege nobody can decode.

**Where prod loads skills from** (2026-09-14): `SKILLS_DIRS=/skills` in the
`eventsourced-config` ConfigMap, and the Dockerfile's runtime stage bakes the repo's `skills/`
directory there (`COPY --from=build /src/skills /skills`) — baked rather than a ConfigMap mount
because a skill grants/denies capability families, and the registry is immutable after
`LoadDirs`, so "which skills is prod serving" should have one answer: the commit the image was
built from. A bad skill file (or a duplicate id, or a dir skill shadowing a built-in) is a FATAL
boot error, so `internal/skills/deploy_test.go` loads the shipped `skills/` dir at commit time —
the same step that would crash-loop the pod — and pins `SKILLS_DIRS` against that COPY
destination, because a path mismatch is the one SILENT failure (a missing dir is ignored by
design, leaving built-ins only). Note `.dockerignore`'s `*.md` does NOT strip `skills/*.md`
(verified: patterns without `/` match top-level paths only), so the COPY works unchanged.

**Inline instructions** (2026-09-14): the lightweight path next to a skill — a free-text
behavior block that needs no skill file, registry entry or digest.
`SessionContextUpdate.Instructions` → `domain.SessionContextUpdated.Instructions`, folded onto
`SessionState.Instructions` (`applyInstructions`) and composed by `Loop.systemPrompt` as a
`[SESSION INSTRUCTIONS]` section AFTER the behavior slot (`instructionsBlock`): a skill
supplies the policy and the linked capabilities, the block supplies the words, and they do not
exclude each other. It is deliberately DURABLE — the block must be in the stream or replay
stops reproducing the prompt and the prefix key becomes unpredictable — and deliberately NOT a
metadata extra, so a long fragment cannot bloat the envelope of every later event
(`applyInstructions` clears it; `sessionContextClearKeys["instructions"]` maps onto "" exactly
like `toolset`). Because it is a system-prompt section and never a conversation turn, compaction
cannot summarize it away — which is what it has over saying the same thing in a user message.
Empty = unchanged, so an unrelated update leaves it alone; clear with `{"clear":["instructions"]}`;
bounded by `MaxSessionInstructionsChars` (8000, HTTP 400 `errInstructionsTooLong`). It rides in
the system digest, so switching it reads as a prefix-key mismatch — a fork then takes the cold
seed instead of betting on a cache it cannot hit. UI: the Behavior popover carries the editor
(draft resyncs from the fold, Save / Clear post `{instructions}` / `{clear:["instructions"]}`),
fed by `replay.instructions`. The popover and its editor are
`packages/ui/src/components/chat/BehaviorPicker.tsx`: it owns the draft/dirty/too-long triple
and the skill list, while the composer keeps what is wire-specific (`handleSelectBehavior`'s
mode-vs-skill distinction, the durable write) and passes both in — the first cut of the
composer split, whose remaining seams are the workspace-binding picker, the `@` search panel
and the toolbar; `ModelPicker` (lane + thinking level) is the same shape and is stateless,
reading the folded lane/level so its button cannot drift. Tests:
`internal/orchestrator/instructions_test.go` (fold/clear/limits, composition order, never-a-turn
+ survives compaction, prefix key, wire shape) and `skill_round_test.go` (the round-level skill
pin, `GET /api/skills`, and a policy matrix over `skills.Builtin().List()` so a new built-in
cannot ship unenforced).

**Capability opt-in is configurable** (`AGENTS_FILE` → `capabilities.opt_in`, example at
`agents.example.yaml`; 2026-09-15): `domain.optInCapabilities`
(`harness.read`/`harness.write`) is the compiled default of "capabilities NO session holds
unless a skill grants them" — the mechanism that links a tool FAMILY to a behavior.
`agentconfig.Capabilities` (a pointer, so "section absent" ≠ "present but empty") overrides it:
`opt_in` absent keeps the compiled list, `opt_in: []` makes everything baseline, a list
replaces it wholesale (normalized like a skill's `grant_capabilities`). It reaches evaluation
without touching `domain`: `capability.SessionPolicy.WithOptIn` holds the set (`nil` = no-op,
non-nil incl. empty = authoritative), and `Loop.capabilityPolicy` applies
`Loop.Agents.Capabilities.OptIn` to the one policy both capability boundaries build — the
offer filter (`filterSkillTools`) and the dispatch-time check (`skillToolCallPolicy`), so the
two can never disagree; `Loop.isOptInCapability` gives the same answer to the spawn-time
parent-held rule (`resolveSubtaskPolicy`), which would otherwise keep demanding a parent hold
for a capability the override made baseline. It is the only knob here that needs no rebuild: skills/modes already
carry per-session grants/denies, worker `CapabilityDefaults` are env-driven. Audit of the
surface (2026-09-15): code-worker tools, orchestrator + harness builtins, MCP (`mcp.<category>`),
worker-web (`network.fetch`/`browser.control`) and worker-browser (`browser.control`) all
declare capabilities, pinned by `TestBuiltinsDeclareRequiredCapabilities` (now incl.
`harnessTools`), `code/capabilities_test.go` and the `capability`/`skill_round`/`mode_skill`
tests; `cmd/worker-tools`' demo `echo` is the only declared tool with none. Worker
`CapabilityDefaults` (RequireApproval/Deny) are announced, folded and shown in the UI decision
view (`sessionstate.go`'s `capability.Evaluate`) but are NOT enforced at execution — the
evaluator is still the observational/UI half of the rollout.

## Auth (2026-09-08): OIDC gating via users.k6n.net

Every application request needs an authenticated principal when auth is
enabled — **reads included** (`internal/auth/browser.go`'s `Browser.Middleware`
wraps the whole handler; only `/healthz`, `/auth/*` and the temporary `/review/`
mirror are public, because transcripts, worker inventory and the live stream are
not public data). Mutating methods do NOT have a separate gate. Issuer is
`https://users.k6n.net` (go-auth, see
its `/agents.md`) — the browser does authorization-code + PKCE against the
confidential client `eventsourced-ai` (redirect URIs
`https://event-agent.k6n.net/auth/callback` + localhost dev variants), the
orchestrator exchanges the
code, keeps server-side sessions behind the `eai_session` HttpOnly cookie, and
silently refreshes via the rotating refresh token. Bearer JWTs are also
accepted (programmatic callers). `internal/auth/` is a vendored copy of
`platform/auth` (auth.go/oidc.go/middleware.go — the platform module is not
separately fetchable; it lives under `platform/` in the ecommerce monorepo)
plus `browser.go` (our session layer). Enabled by `OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` (env
via the `dev/eventsourced-auth` Secret, referenced in
`deploy/k8s/orchestrator.yaml` envFrom); unset → API fully open (dev/tests).
web/nginx.conf proxies `/auth/` to the orchestrator; the SPA redirects to
`/auth/login` on any 401 (`web/src/api.ts`). Secret was minted via the
go-auth MCP `create_client`; rotate with `update_client` + `rotate_secret`.

**CLI sign-in (2026-09-16)**: `cmd/dev-instance` authenticates with the same
issuer over the RFC 8628 **device flow** (`dev-instance login`, reusing
`internal/adapters/mcpoauth` — the flow the MCP workers already use, extended
with `ClientSecret` and a non-interactive `EnsureValid` so a command that cannot
show a user a code gets `ErrLoginRequired` instead of a prompt). The token lands
in `~/.config/dev-instance/token.json` (0600) and is refreshed silently within
2 minutes of expiry; `~/.config/dev-instance/config.json` remembers the
connection and sign-in settings (`dev-instance config`), with precedence flag >
env > file > default — with ONE exception, the credential itself:
`resolveToken` sends `--token` first, then the stored sign-in, then
`DEV_INSTANCE_TOKEN`/`ORCHESTRATOR_TOKEN`. The stored token outranking the
environment is the fix for a stale export shadowing a valid sign-in (every
command 401'd while `whoami` — reading the file — reported a healthy user); the
env vars remain the answer when there is no token file, which is what CI uses.
`whoami` resolves through the same backend, so it inspects the credential the
commands actually send. The client's `audience` must equal the orchestrator's
`OIDC_AUDIENCE` (`https://event-agent.k6n.net`) or the middleware refuses the
token.

The CLI signs in as **`eventsourced-cli`**, a PUBLIC client (2026-09-16),
registered in go-auth via its MCP `create_client` with `is_public: true`, the
same audience/scopes as `eventsourced-ai`, and the same `roles → groups`
claim mapping. The default used to be `eventsourced-ai`, and that cannot work:
that client is CONFIDENTIAL (`has_secret: true`), and go-auth's
authenticateClient refuses a device authorization that names a secret-bearing
client without presenting the secret — so plain `dev-instance login` failed
with `invalid_client`. A device flow has nowhere to put a secret, which is
exactly why the CLI needs its own public client rather than the dashboard's.
The other two paths still exist for anyone who wants them: name a confidential
client and bring its secret (`--client-secret-command`), or use
`--device-clientless` with `AUTH_DEVICE_CLIENT_ID=eventsourced-ai` on the auth
deployment (currently unset). Clientless exists
because go-auth's standard token endpoint requires a named,
secret-authenticated client, so the poll and refresh go to its companion device
endpoints (`/api/auth/device/token`, `/api/auth/device/refresh`, outside the
discovery document) — see go-auth's `internal/oidc/{device.go,oidc.go}`.
`dev-instance whoami` checks acceptance against the API instead of guessing. The
API is reachable as-is through the web ingress
(`https://event-agent.k6n.net/api/...`), so no port-forward is required.

**In-cluster defaults (2026-09-17)**: `defaultOrchestratorURL` and
`defaultNamespace` both read the projected service-account namespace FILE
(`/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace`) — the shell that
runs this binary in a worker pod is a `su - developer` login shell, which drops
the injected `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST`, so a file is the only signal that
survives. They must read the SAME one: with just the injected variable, the URL
resolved the pod's real namespace while `--namespace` stayed `dev`, and every
kubectl-backed command (connect/ssh/logs/code) then addressed the wrong
namespace. `rememberDefaults` compares against the RESOLVED default, so a
derived namespace is never written to `config.json` as if it were a choice.

**Shell completion (2026-09-17)**: `dev-instance completion zsh` prints a
`#compdef` script, and a hidden `dev-instance __complete <kind>` supplies the
VALUES (`instances`, `deployments`, `repos`, `config-keys`) — commands and flags
are static and live in the script, values live in the cluster. The script
forwards the connection flags already on the command line (`--backend`, `--url`,
`--namespace`, `--context`, `--worker-name-prefix`, `--k8s-url`; never a token)
so completion asks the same backend the command will, and only a COMPLETED
flag+value pair travels (`(( i + 1 < CURRENT ))`) — mid-typing a value, the next
word is the empty cursor word and forwarding it alone would make the value
swallow `__complete`. `completionCommands()` in `completion.go` is the one data
list the script is rendered from, and a test pins the command set so a new
command cannot be invisible to TAB. `__complete` is the one command that must be
infallible and fast: exit 0 always, nothing on stderr, a `completeTimeout` (3s)
budget, values cached 5 minutes under `os.UserCacheDir()`
(`dev-instance/complete-<kind>.txt`, written temp+rename) and a stale list beats
none — a completion must never hang a prompt or scribble in it. It reuses
`opsForWithTimeout` (the browser seam with a completion-sized token budget) and
`configKeyList()`. Tests drive the generated script through a real `zsh`
(`-n` for syntax, plus a stub-CLI harness asserting which `__complete` call each
word produces) and skip when zsh is absent; only zsh is supported, because a
shell whose script nobody tested is a guess shipped as a feature.

**Docker in a worker + the VS Code tunnel (2026-09-16)**: two ways into a
worker that used to need cluster surgery, both driven from `dev-instance`.

*Docker*: `mount_docker_socket` on `ports.StartInstanceRequest` (the `docker`
alias for builtin/API callers, `provision_worker`'s `docker` arg,
`dev-instance start --docker`) is the per-instance opt-in, resolved against the
operator default `WORKER_MOUNT_DOCKER_SOCKET` (**off** in the ConfigMap) by
`Controller.wantsDockerSocket` — the request wins in BOTH directions, and an
ABSENT field takes the default (`*bool`, never false-by-omission). The mount
and the SCHEDULING are one decision: a `/var/run/docker.sock` mount is a
`Socket` hostPath, so it only resolves on a node running dockerd and kills the
pod everywhere else — hence `ControllerOptions.DockerNodeSelector`
(`WORKER_DOCKER_NODE_SELECTOR`, the label the dockerd hosts carry), applied
ONLY to the pods that take the socket. One host is a narrower label
(`kubernetes.io/hostname=<node>`), so there is no separate hostname knob; an
empty selector leaves scheduling alone (only sound when every schedulable node
has the socket). `k8s.PodSpec.NodeSelector` is what carries it. `cmd/dev-instance`
is a second caller of the same controller for `--backend k8s`, so it reads both
knobs through `config.ParseLabelSelector` (one parser, not two) — and it reads
them from its OWN environment, which a pod does not get, which is why the HTTP
backend (the default) is the right way to ask from inside a worker. Tests
exercise all of it against the fake k8s client: mount+pin, per-instance opt-in,
explicit opt-out, and no-selector, plus the tri-state wire shape in
`ports`/`instance_tools_test.go`.

*Direct ssh*: every code worker also gets a **LoadBalancer Service on its
pod's sshd** (`WORKER_SSH_LB`, on; `Controller.ensureSSHService`), so a worker
has a stable address that outlives any command — the alternative was a kubectl
port-forward, i.e. an address that changes every run. `dev-instance sshconfig
[--instance-id ID]` reads the address (`ManagedInstance.SSH`, also in
`GET /api/controller/instances`) and writes ONE marker-delimited
`~/.ssh/config` block (alias, address, user, `IdentityFile` = the secret's key
copied to `~/.ssh/dev-instance/<alias>.key`, host keys deliberately NOT pinned
because every pod recreation replaces them), leaving the rest of the file
byte-for-byte alone; `--list`/`--remove` manage exactly what it wrote. That
entry is also the target for `herdr --remote <alias>` (Herdr's remote mode is an
ssh host it boots its server into), which is the reason this exists. Service
details that matter: `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` (the worker runs on ONE
node, so `Local` would drop connections sent to any other — the gitea-style
failure), selector `app=<deployment>` so it follows pod restarts, created after
the deployment and reported like a failed wait (`SSHServiceFailed`), never
recreated while it exists (a new address would invalidate a live config entry),
deleted with the instance on stop, and skipped by `UnexposeInstance` (its
selector also matches the ssh Service; unexposing a dev port must not cut the
operator's way in). **Who authorizes what** (2026-09-17): the Service was never
the problem — the pod authorized NOTHING, so LoadBalancer ssh (and
`herdr --remote`) fell through to the image's password while only
`dev-instance ssh` worked, because that path installs the key itself over
`kubectl exec` (`installAuthorizedKey`) and masked the gap. Cause: the base
image authorizes keys only from the environment
(`DEFAULT_SSH_PUBLIC_KEY`/`SSH_PUBLIC_KEY`/`SSH_AUTHORIZED_KEYS`), a
controller-rendered worker pod sets none of them and has NO `envFrom`, and the
mounted `/secrets/ssh` key is a CLIENT credential (the wrapper copies it into
~/.ssh so the pod can git over ssh) — nothing ever wrote `authorized_keys`.
Fixed on both sides: `scripts/worker-entrypoint.sh` now authorizes the public
half of every private key in the ssh secret (derived with `ssh-keygen -y`, so
the secret still needs no `.pub`; stdin is /dev/null so an encrypted key cannot
block pod start) plus any `authorized_keys`/`*.pub` in the same mount, and the
controller injects the base image's `SSH_PUBLIC_KEY` from
`ControllerOptions.SSHPublicKeySecretName/Key` (`WORKER_SSH_PUBLIC_KEY_SECRET`/
`_KEY`, default `dev-machine-secret`/`SSH_PUBLIC_KEY` — one Secret as the
rotation point for the dev-machine deployment and every worker). The reference
is Optional, so a cluster without that Secret is unchanged. The wrapper runs
BEFORE the base entrypoint, and both only ever append (`>>` behind a
`grep -Fq` guard), so the two key sources accumulate instead of replacing each
other. **On-demand pair** (2026-09-17): the at-start publish does
not retrofit a live worker — `WORKER_SSH_LB` off leaves an existing worker with
no Service, and re-provisioning it costs the pod, its shells and its
uncommitted checkout — so `Controller.ExposeSSH`/`UnexposeSSH` (behind
`dev-instance ssh-expose`/`ssh-unexpose` and
`POST /api/controller/instances/ssh/expose|unexpose`, browser keys `E`/`U`) do
it per worker through the same `findDeploymentForInstance` + worker/repo
authorization as every other instance op, via `Loop.exposeSSHInstance`/
`unexposeSSHInstance` and the shared `authorizeInstanceTarget` +
`resolveInstanceTargetID` helpers. An explicit request wins over the operator
default (the `MountDockerSocket` rule) so `sshServiceFor` is option-free and
`ensureSSHService` is the only default-checking caller; re-exposing an existing
Service returns its address untouched (never re-created), unexposing deletes
only a Service carrying `eventsourced.ai/ssh-service` and releases the address
(a later expose mints a NEW one, so a stale config entry must be rewritten),
missing is not an error, and an `mcp` worker — which runs no sshd — is refused
by name instead of getting an address nothing can accept.

*Tunnel*: `dev-instance code` (alias `tunnel`, browser key `t`) runs
`code tunnel` INSIDE a worker pod via `kubectl exec`, so VS Code connects by
name with nothing forwarded and no ingress. Two non-obvious requirements, both
handled: the CLI must be forced onto the file keychain
(`VSCODE_CLI_USE_FILE_KEYCHAIN`/`..._DISABLE_KEYCHAIN_ENCRYPT`, now image ENV in
the dev-machine image because the start is not from a login shell — a pod has no
D-Bus secret service, so otherwise the token cannot be stored at all), and the
keychain export must be repeated inside the `su -`, which resets the
environment. The start is **detached**: `nohup code tunnel … &`, pid written to
`~/.vscode/dev-instance-tunnel.pid`, output streamed to the sibling log through
`tail -f` so the device code still reaches the user, and `tunnelScript` decides
when to return from EVIDENCE — the CLI printing its own
`https://vscode.dev/tunnel/<name>` URL — not from the CLI exiting. That is the
fix for "it terminates after login": the VS Code CLI may end itself once the
sign-in lands, and a foreground `exec` then made the whole command look failed
(and a dropped connection would have taken the tunnel with it). A tunnel that
never comes up fails with the CLI's last 20 log lines instead of returning
silently, and Ctrl-C during the sign-in kills the child rather than leaving a
half-logged-in tunnel. `--status` reports the login, whether the pidfile's
process is alive (a tunnel started this way is invisible to `code tunnel
status`) and the log tail; `--stop` kills the recorded pid, then
**`code tunnel kill` exits 0 having stopped nothing** for a tunnel the CLI did
not register itself (verified on a live pod, where the process survived a clean
kill), so it also sweeps the user's leftover processes, scoped to the target
user and skipping its own shell (whose command line contains the pattern being
matched). A dropped connection deliberately leaves the tunnel running: the
session is a VS Code window, and it should outlive the CLI that started it.
`TestTunnelScriptsParseAsShell` runs `bash -n` over both layers (outer script and
the `inner` command handed to `su`), which is what catches a quoting slip
without a cluster.

**dev-machine (the base image)**: three fixes that make the image safe as a
worker base. The entrypoint's authorized-key block no longer bakes the
operator's personal key into the script (`DEFAULT_SSH_PUBLIC_KEY` instead) — the
image is `FROM` for every worker pod, so a literal there authorized that key on
every worker, invisible to `kubectl get secret` and unrotatable; the
dev-machine deployment keeps its key through `SSH_PUBLIC_KEY`, and worker pods
get theirs from the mounted `/secrets/ssh` key plus `dev-instance
connect|ssh`. `k8s/deployment.yaml` pins to the dockerd node for the same
Socket-hostPath reason as above, and says `START_CODE_TUNNEL: "true"` because
the entrypoint starts a tunnel when the flag is true OR `TUNNEL_NAME` is set.

**Callback targeting (2026-09-15)**: `/auth/login?redirect_url=<origin>` lets a
frontend declare its own origin, so a locally run or preview-hosted build can log
in against the ONE shared deployment through a vite/ingress proxy whose Host
handling we do not control — the provider then returns the browser, and the
host-only session cookie, to that origin. Precedence: `OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` (an
operator pin) > the validated `redirect_url` > the request Host.
`OIDC_REDIRECT_ALLOW` (defaults `*://localhost:*`, `*://127.0.0.1:*`,
`https://*.preview.k6n.net`) lists the origins allowed to do this; the request's
own origin is always accepted implicitly, so production needs no entry, and
anything else is a 400 — the guard that keeps this from being an open redirect.
The chosen callback rides in the state cookie, so the token exchange presents
the same `redirect_uri` the authorize step used even when the proxy rewrites
Host in one direction only. `?return_to=<relative path>` (same-origin path only;
scheme, `//host`, backslashes and `/auth/*` are dropped, silently — a bad deep
link must not block a login) preserves a deep link across the round trip. Both
params come from `loginURL()` (`packages/ui/src/api.ts`). Every origin in
`OIDC_REDIRECT_ALLOW` must ALSO be registered on the go-auth client: the issuer
validates the callback, so the Go-side allowlist cannot widen what the provider
accepts.
TEMPORARY hole: `GET /review/sessions[...]/debug|replay` mirrors are public
(`publicPath` allows the `/review/` prefix, `internal/auth/browser.go`) for
session-review tooling — lock down once that tooling authenticates.
