**Phase 7 shipped (2026-09-18): the AuthServer spec's provider-wide settings
are consumed.** `effectiveconfig.ProviderSettings` (`provider.go` — issuer,
the four TTLs, session cookie domain, CORS origins, TOTP required, rate
limit max/window/hops, device flow TTLs + clientless id, guest TTL/requests,
WebAuthn name/signCount; duration STRINGS like the CRD) rides the snapshot:
the operator's `ConvertProvider` projects `AuthServerSpec` into it,
`BuildBundleData` publishes it in the bundle's `config.json` under the
`provider` key (omitted when empty — old bundles and old pods stay
compatible), and it is covered by the **revision hash** — a spec-only edit
bumps the revision so `DecidePublish` re-publishes (pointer set-ness is
hashed too: absent → explicit-false is a real change). On the serving pod,
`Snapshot.ApplyToOIDCConfig` overlays the block onto the loaded env config
BEFORE `oidc.New` (stated field wins, absent field leaves env/default;
reported as one "provider settings applied" boot log line), and
every provider setting is **hot-applied** on each snapshot swap:
`effHolder.SetSwapHook` (main.go) reloads the env config, overlays the
bundle's provider block (`Snapshot.ApplyToOIDCConfig`) and calls
`oidc.Server.ApplyConfig`, which swaps the RWMutex-guarded live config and
rebuilds the derived bits — per-IP limiters, refresh/device TTLs — so TTLs,
CORS, rate limits, device flow, guest policy, the TOTP policy and (via main)
the WireGuard client take effect without a restart (CORS and the limiters are
looked up per request; `oidc.Server.config()` guards every read). The WebAuthn
RP name/signCount are baked into the RP at startup and still need a restart. `spec.totp.attempts` and `spec.wireguard` (url **and** the API-key
Secret, resolved by `ResolveServerSecrets` and spliced into config.json like
client secrets) are now carried too, and so is `spec.email` (sender, from,
relay, username and the SMTP password from `smtpSecretRef`) — mail settings
now come from the CRD like everything else, applied at STARTUP (the sender
object is built once; unlike the oidc config there is nothing to swap under a
lock), so changing them needs a pod restart. **The swap-hook log splits the two
views** — `ApplyReport.HotNames()` is what a publish really applies live and
`StartupOnlyNames()` is what it cannot — because naming an email field as
hot-applied is precisely the lie an operator would chase next. `Names()` is
still the startup view, and `TestApplyReportSplitsStartupOnlyFromHot` pins
`Names() == HotNames() + StartupOnlyNames()` so a new field cannot drift into
the wrong half.

**The rule for Secret VALUES, stated plainly:** a value rides the bundle when
it belongs to a DECLARED resource — a client secret, `spec.wireguard.apiKeySecretRef`,
`spec.email.smtpSecretRef`. Those endpoints are then fully CRD-controlled and
need no env var on the pod. What deliberately does NOT ride: `spec.secrets`
(totpWrapKey / secretsWrapKey / tokenSecret / bootstrapAdmin), which the
operator resolves for VALIDATION ONLY (a bad reference reports Degraded)
because those must outlive any configuration change — tie the wrap key to a
publish and a bad reference blanks a key that decrypts stored data. They stay
env-injected from `stack-secrets`.

**API keys are CRDs (2026-09-18):** `AuthAPIKey` + `AuthAPIKeyRequest` make
`/data/apikeys.json` — the last credential store with neither a declared
resource nor an admin UI — a managed one. `internal/operator/apikeys.go`
projects an `AuthAPIKey` onto `platform/auth.APIKey` (the SAME type the
platform's KeyStore parses, so no translation layer can drift), the operator
publishes `apikeys.json` as a FOURTH `auth-effective` key, and the pod's
`AUTH_APIKEYS_FILE` points at that projected file — mcpauth reads exactly what
the CRDs declare. `api/v1alpha1/authapikey_types.go` carries no Secret
reference anywhere, and that is the interesting design difference from
AuthClient: an API key's plaintext is generated by the console, shown once and
stored NOWHERE (the shared file has always kept only SHA-256 digests at 0644,
and a 192-bit random preimage is not recoverable), so there is nothing to
deliver to anyone and nothing to keep in a Secret. The recorded `hash` is
one-way, which is why the CRD can hold it.

The console surface is `internal/admin/apikeys.go` (`GET/POST
/api/admin/apikeys`, `DELETE /api/admin/apikeys/{id}`): file mode mints into
the platform's own KeyStore; Kubernetes mode files `AuthAPIKeyRequest` (one
object per key id, name derived from `spec.id` exactly like client edits) and
returns the plaintext once. Keys are NAMESPACE-scoped, not selector-bound —
the bundle they feed is one per namespace — so `SelectAPIKeys` takes every key
in the server's namespace and `MapChangedObject` maps an `authapikey` change
to every server there. `internal/admin/apikeys_test.go` pins the property that
matters: the value the console hands out authenticates against
`platform/auth.APIKeyAuth` once the record is published.

**Runtime config changes persist on the CRDs (2026-09-18):** the serving pod
has no write access to `AuthServer`, so a runtime change is expressed as an
`AuthConfigRequest` (new CRD, `api/v1alpha1/authconfigrequest_types.go`) and
the **operator** is its only writer — the request reconciler
(`controllers/authconfigrequest_controller.go`, pure merge in
`internal/operator/configrequest.go`) patches the AuthServer spec, and the
snapshot swap hot-applies it. The pod files requests through
`internal/k8sconfig` (stdlib in-cluster client, RBAC create plus
patch-by-resourceName on the one object it owns); the admin console's 2FA
toggle uses it in bundle mode
(202 Accepted; `policyMutable:true`), falls back to the old refusal when no
in-cluster write path is present. Nothing is written to `policy.json` in
bundle mode. Deployment (wired 2026-09-18 in the monorepo
`deploy/k8s/44-auth.yaml` + `44a-auth-operator.yaml`): the serving pod gets
its own `auth` ServiceAccount/RoleBinding and a Role granting create +
`patch` (resourceNames `auth-settings`) on `authconfigrequests`, the pod spec
sets `serviceAccountName: auth` and `POD_NAMESPACE` (downward API), and the
operator Role gained read/watch on `authconfigrequests`, update/patch on
`authservers` and write on `authconfigrequests/status`. Without the pod Role
the toggle answers 502 (the request is never filed); without the operator's,
the request is filed and never applied. All of that RBAC + the
`AuthConfigRequest` CRD are **applied** as of 2026-09-18 (the CRD by hand:
CI does not apply CRDs — see the runbook; the serving pod's Role is exactly
create plus patch-by-name, verified with `kubectl auth can-i`). CI now restarts **both** deployments (`.gitea/workflows/build-push.yml`):
the operator runs the same image from its own Deployment, so rolling only
`auth` left it on the previous binary — silently, since a pod that is never
recreated never pulls a new `:latest`. Consequence to remember: apply the
CRDs *before* rolling out an operator image that watches a new kind, because
controller-runtime exits at startup when a watched CRD is absent.

**The console can edit clients in Kubernetes mode (2026-09-18).** The Client
Registry view used to be read-only there (409, "managed by Kubernetes"); a
client edit now takes the same route as the 2FA toggle — the pod files a
request, the operator writes the resource:

- **`AuthClientRequest`** (new CRD, `api/v1alpha1/authclientrequest_types.go`)
is **one object per client**, named by the shared sanitizer, carrying the
client's desired fields in full (the form submits everything it renders) plus
`delete`, `secretValue` and `clearSecret`. One object per client is the whole
concurrency story: two edits to two clients cannot clobber each other, and
re-filing the same edit patches the same object.
- **`internal/k8snames`** is why the name can be derived on both sides: a
new leaf package (no Kubernetes imports) holding `Sanitize(clientID)` — the
rule `cmd/authmigrate` always used, now shared with the operator (which names
the AuthClient) and the pod writer (which names the request).
`internal/k8snames/names_test.go` pins it against the live registry's real
ids. **Do not fork this rule**: a divergence means the console files a request
the operator resolves to a different client.
- **`internal/operator/clientrequest.go`** is the pure half
(projection/validation/labels/secretRef/change detection) and
**`controllers/authclientrequest_controller.go`** the plumbing. The operator
labels what it creates from the target AuthServer's `clientSelector` — an
unlabelled client would be written and never selected, so the console would
save "successfully" and show nothing. Upserts require the name convention and
refuse a `clientID` another AuthClient already uses (better a request status
than a Degraded AuthServer); **delete resolves by `spec.clientID`**, so a
hand-named resource is still removed rather than silently no-op'd.
- **The client secret passes through the request and does not stay there:**
the operator writes `spec.secretValue` into `auth-client-secrets` (key = the
sanitized client name), points `spec.secretRef` at it, then clears the field.
An ordinary edit preserves the existing `secretRef`, so renaming a client
cannot silently make it public. The pod has **no Secret access at all**; the
operator's grant is name-scoped, and it does not `create` that Secret (the
deployer bootstraps it — `cmd/authmigrate` generates it).
- **The console is told, not made to guess:** `GET /api/admin/clients` serves
`mutable` (an edit can persist) and `managed` (it is the operator applying
it), and a filed edit answers **202 + `pending`** with the submitted view, so
the UI shows "filed for the operator" instead of showing a stale list as if
the save was lost. `clientInput` → CRD spec lives in
`internal/admin/clientrequest.go`.
- **Pending changes are VISIBLE (`internal/admin/pending.go`,
`GET /api/admin/pending`).** A save is not instant, and the gap is not a
second: the operator applies and republishes in about a second, but the pod
only sees the new bundle when the kubelet reprojects the mounted Secret —
measured live 2026-09-18 at **~10 s for one publish and ~70 s for the next**.
So the console keeps an in-memory ledger of what it filed and serves each row
with a state (`pending` → `stale` after 3 min, dropped at 15 min; one row per
(kind, target)), and `web/admin/src/components/Pending.tsx` renders it in the
Client Registry and above the Login Policy card. Do not replace it with a
`setTimeout(reload, …)` — the lag is not bounded at a second, and a fixed
delay makes a working save look lost.
  - **Confirmation is "the served record MOVED", not "the served record
    matches what was submitted".** The operator normalizes (trims, drops
    empty lists), so comparing against the submitted form would report its
    own normalization as "never applied". A create is confirmed by the
    client appearing, a delete by its absence, an edit by its fingerprint
    changing (the fingerprint includes a HASH of the secret, so a secret-only
    rotation counts).
  - **A refusal looks like a change that never arrives.** The pod cannot read
the operator's verdict: its grant on the request resources is write-only
(create + patch, no read) and deliberately so, because a GET returns the
whole object including `spec.secretValue`. Hence `stale` — which points the
operator at the request's own status instead of pretending to know.
  - The ledger is in memory (empty after a restart) and per-pod. In file mode
    nothing is ever recorded; the write already happened.
- **Verify:** `kubectl get authcreq -n ecommerce` (Applied/ClientName/Message
per request) and `kubectl get authclient -n ecommerce` (the result).

**The provider settings LEFT the deployment manifest (2026-09-18):**
`deploy/k8s/44-auth.yaml` carries the moved settings as COMMENTED lines now —
issuer, both token TTLs, the cookie domain, `ALLOWED_ORIGINS`,
`AUTH_RATELIMIT_MAX`, the `AUTH_EMAIL_*` trio and both WireGuard vars — and
`config/migrate/authserver.yaml` states them on the `auth` resource instead
(issuer, TTLs, allowedOrigins, `rateLimit` max 60 + window 1m + one trusted
hop, `email` sender log, `wireguard` url + key SecretRef, plus the already
ported sessionCookieDomain). Two consequences worth remembering: an env value
still stands whenever the spec omits the field, so the commented lines ARE the
rollback; and the spec has to be applied BEFORE the manifest, or a pod restart
would briefly run without the setting. `spec.email` only reaches the pod
once the operator carries it, so a deployment whose operator predates that
will simply keep using the env values (observed live: the spec applied, the
bundle unchanged for mail, env still serving it).

Remaining plan phases: shadow mode (Phase 4 — compare via

## Build / test

- Plain Go module, stdlib-only + the published `git.k6n.net/mats/platform`
  seam (`require`, no `replace`). No cgo. ONE deliberate build tag: `k8s`
  (controllers/ + cmd/auth-operator, the controller-runtime reconciler —
  see the Phase 3 note): `go build ./...` compiles the server, and the
  Dockerfile compiles the operator into the same image.
- **Known gap: a standalone checkout does not build today.** go.sum has no
  hashes for the k8s.io/controller-runtime module set, and the default
  `-mod=readonly` refuses rather than fetching them. Verified at HEAD with
  the workspace off: `GOWORK=off go build ./...` fails on "missing go.sum
  entry" for every target, `./cmd/auth` included — it builds here only
  through the monorepo's root `go.work`. Fix, on a networked machine, then
  commit go.sum: `go mod tidy` (the same command the Dockerfile runs).
- Standalone: `make setup` once, then `go test ./...` / `make build`
  (once the go.sum tidy above has run).
  `platform` is private and sits behind no module proxy, so `make setup`
  installs the `https://git.k6n.net/` → `git@git.k6n.net:` rewrite and
  `GOPRIVATE=git.k6n.net` is what lets Go fetch it at all.
- Inside the monorepo the root `go.work` `use`s `./platform`, so the local
  platform tree wins over the pin; the module is still in `make test-all`'s
  `TEST_MODULES`.

## Storage conventions

- AOF at `<AUTH_DATA_DIR>/auth.aof` (`AUTH_DATA_DIR`, default `/data`).
  Records are `{"op":"set"|"del","key":...,"body":...}` JSONL — the same
  wire shape family as tracking's AOF records.
- Compaction runs at boot only (plan D5), folds to final state per key
  (last set wins, dels drop, del-before-set is a no-op).
- Malformed trailing lines are skipped with a log + `Stats().ReplayErrors`
  rather than failing boot.

## Cross-project seams

- **`platform/auth`** — the verification seam. go-auth only *mints*; every
  consumer already verifies (the P1 test suite proves it via `auth.NewOIDC`
  against a real HTTP server). **The RFC 8628 device flow is served here now**
  (plan §5.10/P5): go-auth is the canonical issuer, the backoffice keeps its
  own copy untouched, and a device gets an ordinary RS256 go-auth token — not
  a platform HS256 device token. See the device section below and
  `docs/companion-app.md` for the client side.
- **Platform pin** — `platform` is developed in the monorepo and published
  from it (`make publish-platform VERSION=v0.x.y` at the repo root pushes
  `platform/` to `git.k6n.net/mats/platform` and tags it). Bump this repo's
  pin whenever a mint-side change has to move together with the verifier — a
  stale pin is the one way this service can silently diverge from every
  consumer that verifies its tokens.

  grant with rotation (`AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL`) — SPA cutover (P6) pieces.
  `AUTH_ISSUER` override not set in dev (derived from Host).
- **`backoffice`** — hosts the OIDC client (SPA + server flow) this service
  will serve from P6 cutover; hosts the device approve page.

## Device authorization grant (2026-09-11, plan P5)

The companion-app flow is now served by this issuer, so an app that had no
browser of its own has exactly one auth endpoint to talk to. It is a real
OAuth grant, not a special case: the device receives an ordinary RS256
go-auth access token (+ `id_token` with `auth_time`, + a rotating
`refresh_token`), verified through the same JWKS by every consumer.

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `POST /oauth/v2/device_authorization` | RFC 8628 start: `client_id`, optional `scope`, optional `redirect_url` → `device_code`, `user_code`, `verification_uri`, `verification_uri_complete`, `expires_in`, `interval` |
| `POST /oauth/v2/token` (`urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`) | Poll: `authorization_pending` → `slow_down` → the token, or `access_denied` / `expired_token` / `invalid_grant` |
| `GET /device` | The verify page (pretty, themed): sign in if needed, then approve/deny |
| `GET /device/done` | The completed page (`?ok=1` / `?denied=1`), with a return-to-app countdown when a redirect was given |
| `GET /api/auth/device/info?code=` | What a pending code asks for (the page's live lookup; public, leaks nothing) |
| `POST /api/auth/device/approve` \| `/deny` | The decision — **session + admin role** gated |
| `POST /api/auth/device/refresh` | A fresh token from the device token: the `refresh_token` grant with a JSON body accepted |
| `POST /api/auth/device` \| `/api/auth/device/token` | Compatibility aliases for the companion app's existing paths — pointing the app here is a base-URL change |

Decisions worth remembering:

- **Bearer mode.** The in-repo clients (`cmsctl auth login`, the Android
  ledger app) send no `client_id` at all — only `grant_type`/`device_code`.
  So the aliases accept that shape and treat the unguessable `device_code` /
  `refresh_token` itself as the credential; `AUTH_DEVICE_CLIENT_ID` names the
  client those requests belong to. The RFC-shaped endpoints still authenticate
  a named client. Without that env var, a clientless start is a 400 whose
  message says so.
- **Approval is admin-only** and always interactive: a pending code grants
  nothing until a signed-in admin approves it, and the minted token carries
  *their* identity and roles (same contract as the authorization-code flow).
- **Scopes** are intersected with the client's, silently, like the authorize
  and `client_credentials` grants (a dropped scope is logged). A device only
  receives a `refresh_token` when its client allows `offline_access` **and**
  the request asks for it — the usual reason a device cannot renew.
- **Redirect** (`redirect_url`) is accepted and honoured after approval. Per
  explicit decision any http(s) or custom scheme is allowed for now (a
  companion app's `net.k6n.ledger://` deep link); `javascript:`/`data:`/
  `vbscript:`/`file:` are refused, and the value is passed to the template as
  `template.URL` only after that check. The allowlist config belongs in
  `validateDeviceRedirect` when it lands.
- **Polling discipline**: a client polling inside the advertised `interval`
  gets `slow_down`; grant state is in memory (single replica, short TTL), so a
  restart just means the app starts a new flow.

## WireGuard peer administration (2026-09-11)

The **wireguard-helper** (a separate single-binary Go service on the LAN,
`10.10.1.2:8443`) owns the peer list of an existing `wg0`: key generation, IP
allocation, client-config rendering, and applying peers to the live interface.
go-auth is the **operator front door** for it, not a WireGuard implementation:
the admin UI (`WireGuardView.tsx`) and the MCP tools proxy to the helper with
`AUTH_WIREGUARD_API_KEY`, which stays in this process — a browser or MCP client
authenticates against the ordinary session/admin gate and never sees the key.

Enable by setting both `AUTH_WIREGUARD_URL` (e.g. `http://10.10.1.2:8443`) and
`AUTH_WIREGUARD_API_KEY`. Both unset = the view reports `configured:false`, the
MCP tools answer "not configured", and the service still starts (the helper is
optional infrastructure, unlike the failure-closed sources).

- **Admin API** (session + admin role, same gate as users/clients):
  `GET /api/admin/wireguard` (overview: `configured`, `url`, `peers`, and an
  `error` when the helper is configured but unreachable — deliberately always
  200 so the console can distinguish the two), `POST
  /api/admin/wireguard/users`, `DELETE
  /api/admin/wireguard/users/{name}`, `GET
  /api/admin/wireguard/users/{name}/config` (attachment), `GET
  /api/admin/wireguard/server-config`, `POST /api/admin/wireguard/import`.
- **MCP tools**: `list_wireguard_peers`, `get_wireguard_peer_config`,
  `create_wireguard_peer`, `delete_wireguard_peer`, `import_wireguard_peers`,
  `get_wireguard_server_config`. `create_wireguard_peer` returns the private
  key *and* the rendered client config in one response (the helper reveals the
  private key only once) and reports `apply_error` when the peer was saved but
  the interface was not updated.
- **Status mapping**: the helper's 404/409/400 pass through; anything else
  (unreachable, apply failure) is a 502 — the helper is the upstream and a
  transport failure is not the operator's mistake.
- **Audit**: `admin.wireguard.peer-create`, `admin.wireguard.peer-delete`,
  `admin.wireguard.import` (source `admin` or `mcp`). Peer names are validated
  against path separators, comment markers and control characters
  (`wireguard.ValidateName`) because the name is both a URL path segment and,
  for imported peers, a comment line in the wg-quick config.
- **Imported peers** (`created_at` zero) exist because the helper adopts the
  existing `[Peer]` blocks at startup; their private key lives only on the
  original device, so the helper answers 409 for their client config. Run
  **Import** after editing `wg0.conf` by hand, or the next apply can drop
  those peers.

## Sign-in links (2026-09-12)

Passwordless email sign-in for **everyone**, not just guests. `GET /magic`
renders the request form, `POST /magic` mints a single-use link (15 min,
`reset.Store.IssueLink`, `reset.KindLogin`) and emails it; `GET
/login/link?token=…` consumes it. `/guest/link` is a permanent alias for the
same handler, because admin-issued guest URLs are already in inboxes.

The request side is a deliberate clone of the forgot-password contract
(`internal/oidc/magic.go`): identical answer and redirect for a known and an
unknown address, its **own** per-email budget via `internal/oidc/limiter.go`
(3 per 15 min — separate from `/forgot` so exhausting one does not lock the
other), mail only for an existing usable account, and no sender configured →
silent success. Never add a "no such account" branch here.

The consume side is the security-relevant part, and the rule is that a link
is a **first factor only**:

- approved guest inside their window → straight into a session (unchanged);
- everyone else → `startTOTPLogin`, i.e. the ordinary second-factor gate. On
  a 2FA-mandatory instance this is what stops a magic link being a 2FA
  bypass, and `TestMagicLinkStillOwesSecondFactor` asserts exactly that (no
  session cookie, a `/totp` challenge instead).
- only when 2FA is not required *and* nothing is enrolled does the link
  complete the sign-in itself.

A spent/expired link renders the login page with a re-request hint — no
oracle. Guest links now ride the same store as reset/login links, so the
"no plaintext token in the audit log" property is preserved. Audit:
`login.magic_request`, `login.link`.

Admins can mint + email the same kind of link for a registered user from the
console: `POST /api/admin/users/{id}/magic-link` (`internal/admin/magic.go`)
revokes outstanding links first, refuses disabled accounts and closed guest
windows, audits `admin.user.signin-link`, and returns the URL once in the
response like the invite/guest-link flows (`emailed` reports the send).

## Sessions & device management (2026-09-12)

Self-service "where am I signed in?", owner-scoped like the secret vault
(`internal/oidc/sessions_http.go`, `withUser` = cookie **or** bearer via
`RequestUser`, so a companion app can manage its own sessions with a token):

- `GET /api/sessions` — the user's live browser sessions, newest activity
  first, with a derived `device` label, raw `userAgent`, `ip`, and `current`
  (false for a token caller, which has no browser session).
- `DELETE /api/sessions/{id}` — one device. Revoking the *current* session
  clears the cookie (`revokedCurrent: true`); a foreign id and an unknown id
  both 404, so the handle space is not an oracle.
- `POST /api/sessions/revoke-others` — all but the caller's.
- `POST /api/sessions/revoke-all` — `RevokeGrants`: sessions **and** refresh
  tokens (what a suspected compromise needs).

`Session.ID` is the **public handle** (random 8-byte token); the session
token is the credential and is never returned. Every session now records
`UserAgent` + `IP` at creation (`sessionMeta`), UA capped at 300 chars. Two
honest limits: the store is in-memory so a restart empties the list, and the
list covers browser sessions only — device/access tokens are not sessions and
are revoked by rotating the token secret or signing key. UI: `DevicesCard` in
the Account view.

### Where the session store lives

`internal/session` owns the `Session` type, the in-memory `Store` and
`DeviceLabel` — **not** `internal/oidc`, even though the OIDC flows are where
sessions are born. It moved (2026-09-12) because more than one surface needs
it: the Account view's routes (`oidc/sessions_http.go`) and the MCP session
tools (`mcp/tools_sessions.go`) both list and revoke the same sessions, which
is the same reason `internal/secrets` is its own package. `oidc.Server`
exposes the store via `Sessions()` and keeps the HTTP half (the cookie, the
request metadata, the TTL policy, the guest-window cap) — so a `*session.Store`
can be handed to a surface without exporting anything that resolves a session
from a raw **token**. That is deliberate: the store's API is subject-scoped
(`ListForUser`, `RevokeOne`, `RevokeOthers`, `DeleteForUser`), because the
token is the credential and no other package should be able to turn one into a
session.

There are now **two** entry points to the same state, so keep them in step:
HTTP (`/api/sessions*`, cookie-or-bearer) and MCP (`list_sessions`,
`revoke_session`, `revoke_other_sessions`, `revoke_all_sessions`,
owner-scoped from `reqauth`). They must agree on the audit event
(`audit.SessionRevoked`) and on which bulk revoke reaches refresh tokens:
`revoke-all` does (`RevokeGrants`, injected into `mcp.NewServer`), `revoke-others`
does not. Both are tested for it (`internal/mcp/tools_sessions_test.go`).

## UserInfo + logout (2026-09-12)

Discovery advertised `userinfo_endpoint` and `end_session_endpoint` from the
start while both routes answered 501 (`notImplemented`, with stale "arrives
with P3" notes — P3 shipped long ago). That is the one class of bug a
discovery document is not allowed to have: any standard OIDC library will call
UserInfo and either break or fall back. Both are now real.

**`internal/oidc/userinfo.go`** — `sub` plus the claims the access token's
scopes unlock (`profile` → `name`, `email` → `email`), then the client's
`claim_mapping` + static claims, so UserInfo and the id_token agree.

**`internal/oidc/logout.go`** — RP-initiated logout plus RFC 8471 back-channel
notifications. `internal/login/templates/logout.html` is the confirm /
signed-out page (`login.ServeLogout`). Client registry gained
`post_logout_redirect_uris` and `backchannel_logout_uri` (admin API + the
Client Registry form).

Four decisions here are load-bearing, and each has a test named after it:

1. **`token_use` pins the token type in both directions.** Access tokens are
   `token_use: "access"`, id_tokens `"id"`. Without it, an id_token — RS256,
   same `iss`/`sub`, and held by the relying party — passes as an access token
   at `/api/*` (full user authority for a client whose scopes granted nothing)
   and at UserInfo. `verifyAccessToken` and `verifyIDTokenHint` each enforce
   their side; the check fails closed, so a token minted before this claim is
   refused (access tokens are short-lived deliberately).
2. **No logout without a hint, unless confirmed.** A bare GET with a
   `client_id` is a link an attacker can make a victim click; we render a
   confirmation whose button POSTs back with a CSRF pair. With a hint the
   request is trusted because only we could have signed it — and the hint may
   be *expired*, since people log out long after the token lapses.
3. **The cookie decides whose session ends.** The hint says whose logout this
   is; if the session's subject disagrees, nothing happens. A replayed or
   leaked hint is inert — otherwise the hint's `aud` would be an authority to
   end somebody else's session.
4. **`post_logout_redirect_uris` fails closed.** It is a separate list from
   `redirect_uris` and an empty list means *no redirect*, not "any" — unlike
   `allowsRedirect`, which predates the registry and tolerates empty. A
   permissive default here would make `end_session` an open redirect.

A deliberate exception to exact matching lives in `internal/oidc/redirect.go`: a
registered `redirect_uri` may also be used in its **loopback form** —
`http://localhost:<any port>/<same path>`, likewise `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` — so
a client registered at its production URL can be run on a laptop without a
registry entry per port (`AUTH_LOOPBACK_REDIRECTS`, on by default;
`Config.AllowLoopbackRedirects` in the library defaults to *off*, so only a
configuration that says so is relaxed). Only the host and the port are
widened: the path must equal a registered one exactly (after cleaning, so
`/cb/../x` is not `/cb`), the host must be loopback matched **exactly**
(`localhost.evil.example` and `127.0.0.1.nip.io` are not), and the scheme must
be http or https with no fragment or userinfo. It cannot become an open
redirect because no loopback spelling reaches a remote machine — whatever the
URI says, the browser resolves it on the user's own box — and the local
port-hijack it invites (RFC 8252 §8.1) is already covered by the PKCE every
public client must send, those being the only clients whose intercepted code
would be usable. `TestAllowsLoopbackRedirect` pins the shapes that must *not*
pass, and `TestLoopbackRedirectCompletesTheFlow` runs a whole login against the
loopback form. A second relaxation lives in the same file, and unlike the first
it needs no flag because it cannot happen by accident: a registered
`redirect_uri` whose host is written `*.` covers that whole subtree —
`https://*.preview.k6n.net/auth/callback` accepts
`https://pr-42.preview.k6n.net/auth/callback`. The reason is the same one that
motivates the loopback rule, one level up: the hostnames a preview environment
gets are chosen at run time (`pr-42.preview.k6n.net`, `pr-43.preview.k6n.net`,
…) and there is no list that can enumerate them ahead of the fact, so the
alternative is a registry edit per environment or a `redirect_uris` list that
is stale again by the afternoon. It is the dynamic-DNS shape — the same idea as
the `*.preview` wildcard A record and certificate — applied to the redirect
match, and it widens the host alone: the `*` must be the leading label on its
own (a `*` anywhere else, as in `api.*.example.com` or `ex*mple.com`, is a
literal that matches nothing, so no entry can silently cover more than it
names), the suffix must sit on a label boundary (`evilpreview.k6n.net` is not
`*.preview.k6n.net`, and the bare `preview.k6n.net` is a registration of its
own), the subdomain part must be real labels, and scheme, port, path (cleaned)
and query must equal the registration with no userinfo or fragment — the exact
restrictions the loopback rule applies. `allowsPostLogoutRedirect` consults the
same matcher, so a registered subtree is also a logout return. Two things stay
deliberately out of reach: the request may not contain a `*` of its own (a
wildcard is a fact about the registration, never about what a caller asks for —
even an entry that spells one literally is refused), and a wildcard is never
the *destination* for a client that omitted `redirect_uri`, which is answered
with the first non-wildcard entry (`defaultRedirectURI`) or refused. That last
one is easy to miss: the old code took `redirectURIs[0]` verbatim, which with a
wildcard registration would point the browser at a name that does not resolve.
`TestRedirectURIMatchesSubdomainWildcard` pins both directions,
`TestAllowsWildcardRedirectAndPostLogout` the logout list, and
`TestWildcardRedirectCompletesTheFlow` runs a whole login from a host under the
subtree.

Back-channel fan-out is built from the **session record**, which therefore
remembers the clients it authorized (`session.Store.RememberClient` /
`Clients`, populated at authorize). Read that list *before* deleting the
session — collecting it after silently notifies only the requester, which is
exactly what `TestBackchannelNotifiesEveryClientOfTheSession` catches (a
single-client case cannot: the requester is always told).

Not implemented: front-channel logout. Back-channel is strictly more reliable
and needs no iframe.

## Authentication strength: amr / acr + prompt / max_age / acr_values (2026-09-12)

Tokens now say *how* someone signed in, and authorization requests can demand
it. `internal/authn` is the vocabulary (new package): the RFC 8176 methods
(`pwd`, `otp`, `hwk`, plus `mfa` when more than one factor was used) and the
acr classes — the InCommon IAP URNs `…:iap:bronze` (one factor) and
`…:iap:silver` (more than one), which is what OIDC Core's own examples use.
The short aliases `bronze` / `silver` are accepted on input and normalised on
output.

**One rule keeps the claim and the class from disagreeing:** `mfa` is present
exactly when the sign-in was multi-factor, and `acr` is derived from it
(`authn.ACRFor`). The only way to reach silver is `authn.SecondFactor`
(password → TOTP, link → TOTP, enrollment), which is why a user-verified
passkey reports `[hwk, mfa]` (possession plus verification) while a bare tap on
a security key reports `[hwk]` and stays bronze.

`amr` + `acr` ride on **both** tokens. The id_token is the standard home; the
access token carries them too because a resource server that only ever sees an
access token is exactly the one that wants to enforce "passkey only". They are
*absent* on a `client_credentials` token — no end user authenticated, and
claiming the floor class there would say one did.

**`internal/oidc/authorize_policy.go`** parses `prompt`, `max_age` and
`acr_values` and decides what to do. The decision table:

| Request | Session | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `prompt=none` | none | `error=login_required` at the redirect_uri — **never** a login page |
| `prompt=none` | stale (`max_age`) or too weak (`acr_values`) | `error=interaction_required` |
| `prompt=none` | fine | code (the SPA's "am I still signed in?" path) |
| `prompt=login`, stale `max_age`, `max_age=0` | any | bounce to `/login`, even with a valid session |
| `acr_values=silver` | bronze, account has a second factor | one step-up bounce, then honest bronze |
| `acr_values=silver` | bronze, account has none | straight through, honest bronze |
| `acr_values=bronze` | silver | straight through; the class is a **floor**, not a set |

The round trip is where this can go wrong, so two URL markers bound it. Any
requirement that forced the trip is satisfied by the login that follows:
`prompt` and `max_age` are **stripped** from the pending request before the
bounce (`loginBounceURL`), and `_reauth=1` tells the login page not to take its
"already signed in → straight back" shortcut — without it the browser would
come back and be handed a code without anyone authenticating.
`_acr_stepup=1` makes a class step-up attempt happen **exactly once**: a class
the account cannot reach would otherwise loop forever, since every password
login produces the same bronze session. On the second pass we stop asking and
let the token report the class actually reached (OIDC Core §2 permits a
different acr than requested, and it beats an error for a request the account
could not satisfy).

Not implemented: `prompt=consent` / `select_account` are accepted and ignored
(no per-client consent screen; one account per user), RFC 9470's
`insufficient_user_authentication` challenge on resource servers, and a
`claims` request parameter.

## Request security: PKCE enforcement + response headers (2026-09-13)

**PKCE is now enforced** (RFC 7636). `code_challenge_method` has always had to
be `S256` (`plain` is a downgrade, RFC 7636 §4.4.2), but a challenge used to be
optional even for a client that had nothing else to authenticate with. A
**public client — no registered secret — must now send a challenge**, because
the challenge is the only thing binding an authorization code to the client
that asked for it (RFC 9700 §2.1.1; OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE for every
code-flow client). A confidential client may still skip it. Both PKCE
rejections are delivered as `error=invalid_request` at the client's
`redirect_uri` — the redirect has already been validated at that point, so the
waiting client can surface it instead of showing a bare 400 JSON body.

The predicate is `rc.secret == ""`, i.e. exactly "no secret in the registry"
(`clients.go` already documented the absent field as *public client*). Every
consumer in the monorepo already sends S256: `backoffice-shell/src/auth.ts`
and `slask-finder/pkg/writeradmin/oidcauth.go`.

**Every response carries a security-header set** (`cmd/auth/headers.go`,
applied to the whole mux, so the JSON API and 404s get it too):
`Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`,
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. The host
puts single-use secrets in URLs (`/reset`, `/magic`, `/guest/link`,
`/login/link`), which is what `no-referrer` is for. HSTS is deliberately
*not* re-set here — the ingress already sends it, and two sources would drift.

The CSP is `default-src 'none'` with a short allow-list, and each allowance is
traceable to something the pages load:

| Directive | Why it reads that way |
|---|---|
| `script-src 'self'` | Every page's JS is an embedded asset. **No** `'unsafe-inline'`, so an inline `<script>` cannot be added without noticing — the TOTP enroll page used to have one |
| `style-src … 'unsafe-inline'` | The admin SPA sets React inline styles (`style={{…}}`) and the enroll template uses a `style` attribute. Styles are not the XSS surface; scripts are |
| `style-src https://fonts.googleapis.com`, `font-src https://fonts.gstatic.com` | Inter is loaded from Google Fonts by every template + `web/admin/index.html`. Self-hosting the font would retire both |
| `connect-src 'self'` | The JSON API, `/mcp/sse`, the device-flow polling. Nothing here talks to a third party |
| `img-src 'self' data:` | No external images; the QR is inline SVG (`innerHTML`, not a fetch) |
| `frame-ancestors 'none'` | Nothing frames this host (front-channel logout, the one design that would, is not implemented). `X-Frame-Options: DENY` rides along for pre-Level-2 browsers |

Verified empirically in headless Chrome rather than assumed — same-origin
scripts run, inline style *attributes* apply, the console's `blob:` download
(WireGuard peer config export) is not refused, and a deliberate third-party
resource is blocked. `cmd/auth/headers_test.go` pins the policy directive by
directive, including that `script-src` must never gain `'unsafe-inline'` while
`style-src` keeps it.

## Ingress authentication: go-auth as the auth-url policy point (2026-09-15)

nginx-ingress's `auth-url` annotation runs a **subrequest** before proxying:
200 lets the request through (response headers named in
`auth-response-headers` are copied to the backend), any other status is
returned to the client verbatim. `GET /oauth2/auth` is that policy endpoint,
so an operator annotates any ingress with the auth host and go-auth decides —
no oauth2-proxy sidecar, no per-app code. One endpoint, three credential
modes, decided by what the subrequest carries:

| Mode | Credential | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **session/bearer** | session cookie or `Authorization: Bearer` | `oidc.RequestUser`, the same resolution `/api/*` uses — **checked FIRST**; a signed-in console user (or a companion app's access token) walks through with no second prompt, and no argon2 cost even when the browser also replays a cached Basic header. Cookie/bearer success is silent — it fires per page load |
| **basic** | `Authorization: Basic` (sessionless caller) | `users.Verify` — the account's normal password (curl, Grafana, uptime probes). Failures spend the **shared login throttle** (`loginFailed`/`loginAllowed`) and audit `login.ingress` ok=false; a second allowance would just halve the cost of brute-forcing the same secret at `/login`. A throttled guess is the ordinary **401** challenge, deliberately not audited — NEVER 429, which nginx's auth_request renders as a bare 500. Concurrency is capped (`verifySem`, 2) so page-load-sized bursts cannot stack 64 MiB argon2 allocations past the container limit |
| **challenge** | nothing | `401` + `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="<host>"` (curl prompts, browser retries), and when the realm opts into `browser_redirect` also `Location: <issuer>/login?rd=<original URL>` — the normal login page, returning to the original URL via `validateReturnTo` |

Authenticated-but-not-permitted (the realm's `users` allowlist) is **403**
with its own audit kind, `ingress.denied`, and does NOT touch the login
budget — the caller proved the credential; that is an authorization verdict.
On success the endpoint sets `X-Auth-User` (email) and, when the realm sets
`forward_roles`, `X-Auth-Roles` — the headers `auth-response-headers` copies
to the backend, set by us and never passable by the client.

Realm resolution and the registry (`internal/oidcrealms`):

- **The realm is chosen by `X-Original-URL`'s host**, and the host must be
  an explicitly configured realm — unlisted host (or a subrequest with no
  original URL) is **403 with no oracle and no audit record** (a scanner
  varying Host headers is unauthenticated traffic and must not fill the
  bounded ring). Deliberately no subdomain matching, no "protect
  everything" default: the `browser_redirect` mode echoes `X-Original-URL`
  into a `Location`, and building redirects from that header for hosts the
  operator never named is the road to an open redirect. Host matching is
  exact, case-insensitive, FQDN-trailing-dot tolerant; an explicit `:port`
  realm wins over a portless realm for the same host, and a portless realm
  covers any port ("one host, one door").
- **`AUTH_INGRESS_REALMS`** — a JSON array, the exact `AUTH_CLIENTS`
  contract (mtime reload, fail-closed startup, last-good-state on a bad
  runtime edit): `{"host": "grafana.k6n.net", "browser_redirect": true,
  "forward_roles": true}` or `{"host": "api.k6n.net", "users":
  ["ops@tornberg.me"]}`. When the env is unset the endpoint is **not
  mounted at all** — a 403-to-everything `/oauth2/auth` on deployments that
  do not use the feature is noise and a probe target.

Basic mode is only viable because the auth-request cache lives in nginx:
`auth-cache-key` + `auth-cache-duration` (e.g. `200 60s, 401 5s`) keep the
argon2id burn off the per-request path — `users.Verify` is deliberately
slow, and running it per request is a self-inflicted denial of service. The
endpoint itself has **no per-IP limiter** on purpose: the subrequest carries
the ORIGINAL client's address, so an IP budget here would re-create the
shared-bucket incident (2026-09-13) inside the IdP; nginx's cache is the
rate control. And the auth host's own ingress must never carry an auth-url
annotation — a subrequest that recurses into the controller hangs. Tests:
`internal/oidc/ingauth_test.go` (mode table, throttle sharing, challenge
shapes, bearer/cookie paths, Basic-beats-session) and
`internal/oidcrealms/oidcrealms_test.go` (fail-closed open, host/port
matrix, mtime reload keeping last-good-state).

Not implemented (deliberate): per-ingress secrets (a basic credential IS the
account password — rotate it through the existing flows so the audit trail
stays honest), `/oauth2/logout` for ingress sessions (the console logout
already ends the session the ingress resolves), and POST bodies (nginx never
forwards them to the subrequest — GET only).

## Token exchange: delegation, not impersonation (2026-09-13)

`internal/oidc/token_exchange.go` implements RFC 8693 at the token endpoint.
The motivation is the one gap the static shared secrets (`AUTH_APIKEYS_FILE`,
`MCP_API_KEY`) cannot close: they authenticate a service but record no
identity, so nothing says *which* service did a thing. Exchange lets service A
trade a user's access token for one aimed at service B, carrying
`act: {"sub": "A"}` — "A did this, for that user".

**Impersonation is deliberately unreachable.** `act` is always set, so the
resulting token never merely *is* the user. That is a policy choice, not a
limitation: a token that appears to be the user is the thing that makes audit
trails lie.

The policy (`grantTokenExchange`), each clause for a reason:

| Clause | Why |
|---|---|
| Caller must be **confidential** (registered `secret`) | The grant is "authenticate, then trade"; a public client has nothing to authenticate with. Enforced *in the grant*, because `handleToken` lets secretless clients through to the dispatch |
| `subject_token` must have been issued to the caller (`azp`) | The one check that stops client B redeeming a token it merely saw. `aud` can name several services, so it cannot carry this |
| Subject must be a live, usable **user** | A `client_credentials` token's subject is a client id, so it is refused — machine-to-machine means asking for the audience up front |
| `scope` ⊆ the subject token's scopes | The subject token's scopes are what the user actually authorized; widening is `invalid_scope` |
| `audience`/`resource` aim the token at the receiver | The caller already holds the user's authority; the receiving service decides what it is worth |
| No `refresh_token` in the response | RFC 8693 §2.2.1 — a short-lived, narrowly-aimed exchange must not mint a long-lived credential |
| `requested_subject` refused | Answering a different question than asked is how impersonation bugs start |

**`azp` is new on every access token** (`mintAccess`), and it is
load-bearing here rather than decorative. Adding a claim is safe for
consumers: `platform/auth`'s verifier enforces `iss/aud/exp/nbf` and ignores
the rest, and nothing in the monorepo reads `azp`.

`mint` is now a thin forwarder to `mintAccess(...)`, which takes an
`accessTokenOpts{aud, act}`. That kept all four pre-existing mint call sites
unchanged while letting the exchange override the audience and add the
delegation claim — worth knowing before refactoring either.

A chained exchange (exchanging an already-exchanged token) **nests** `act`
(`act.act`) rather than flattening it, so a multi-hop call still names every
hop. Not implemented: `may_act`, arbitrary `actor_token` (only the caller's
own is accepted, for client interop), non-access-token types, and id_tokens
or refresh tokens as the requested output.

## Local frontend development: the dev auth panel + dev tokens (2026-09-18)

The frontends (`web/admin`, future apps) are developed against a running
go-auth through the Vite proxy — `AUTH_DEV_TARGET` picks the backend, default
`https://users.k6n.net` (README: "Local frontend development"). Because
localhost cannot do passkeys (the RP ID belongs to the issuer) and agents
want bearer tokens rather than cookies, the RFC 8628 device grant doubles as
the dev login. Nothing was added to the server for this — it is the
companion-app flow, reused:

- `web/admin/src/dev/` (DEV-only lazy chunk, so it never reaches the
  production bundle): `devAuth.ts` speaks `/api/auth/device`,
  `/api/auth/device/token` (poll with `slow_down` back-off) and
  `/api/auth/device/refresh`; `DevAuthPanel.tsx` renders it and registers
  `setTokenRefresher` into `api.ts`, which retries a 401 once through it
  before dropping a dead token. The dev refresh token sits under the
  `go-auth.dev.refresh` localStorage key — deliberately dev-only (production
  keeps tokens in sessionStorage), which is why the DEV guard is
  load-bearing.
- `scripts/dev-token.mjs`: the same flow for terminals and agents —
  `login` (prints the approval URL, waits), `token` (fresh access token,
  rotates the stored refresh token, `GO_AUTH_TOKEN` passthrough), `whoami`,
  `forget`. Store: `~/.go-auth/dev/<host>.json`, mode 0600. `make dev-login`
  / `make dev-token` wrap it.
- The one server-side requirement: a clientless device start needs
  `AUTH_DEVICE_CLIENT_ID` (`make dev` defaults it to `dev-console`;
  registry-less deployments resolve any id to the built-in dev client, while
  a registry deployment must name a real one). Tokens minted this way are
  ordinary RS256 access tokens carrying the approving admin's identity —
  `/api/*` accepts them through the cookie-or-bearer path (bearer.go), no
  scope required.

## Deployment

- **Image build + CI live in this repo**: `.gitea/workflows/build-push.yml`
  runs `scripts/build-push.sh` on every push to `main` (docs-only pushes
  skipped), pushes `registry.k6n.net/ecommerce/auth:latest` and rolls out
  `deployment/auth`. There is no longer an `auth` entry in the monorepo's
  `.gitea/workflows/build-push.yml` matrix or `deploy/k8s/detect-changes.sh`.
- **Cluster manifests stay in the monorepo**: `deploy/k8s/44-auth.yaml`
  (Deployment + Service + Ingress for `users.k6n.net`) + the `auth-data` PVC in
  `00-namespace-config.yaml`, and the `deploy/docker-compose.yml` `auth`
  service (`make dev-auth` for a local IdP — it passes `../platform` as the
  BuildKit context). Single replica — the AOF + signing keys are single-writer
  (plan D5); no HPA.
- **Device settings in the cluster**: `44-auth.yaml` carries
  `AUTH_DEVICE_CODE_TTL` / `AUTH_DEVICE_INTERVAL` and a commented
  `AUTH_DEVICE_CLIENT_ID` — set it (and give that client `offline_access` in
  the registry) when a companion app is pointed at this issuer. Compose passes
  the same three through from the host env.
- **WireGuard settings in the cluster**: `44-auth.yaml` sets
  `AUTH_WIREGUARD_URL` and reads `AUTH_WIREGUARD_API_KEY` from
  `stack-secrets` (`optional: true` — absent = the view says "not
  configured"). Add that key to `stack-secrets` before the view is usable;
  compose passes both through from the host env.
- **Live test host: `https://users.k6n.net`** — `AUTH_ISSUER` is set to the
  test host now; at P6 cutover flip it to `https://auth.k6n.net` and float
  the route (cert-manager already issued `users-k6n-tls`).
- **CAUTION:** do not run `kubectl apply -f deploy/k8s/00-namespace-config.yaml`
  against a live cluster with out-of-band `stack-secrets` keys — the
  manifest's `stack-secrets` block only carries dev placeholders, and the
  three-way merge deletes keys added out-of-band (observed 2026-09-01;
  recovered byte-exact from running container specs). Apply the PVC alone
  (`kubectl apply -f -` with just the `auth-data` block) or move the real
  keys into the manifest first.

## Improvement suggestions

- **No durable fsync** — `Append` flushes the bufio writer but relies on the
  OS page cache; a power loss in the window between append and the next
  write can lose the last record(s). Fine for auth-mutation volume; document
  before relying on it in prod, or add periodic `file.Sync`.
- **WebAuthn v1 posture** — `attestation:"none"` (no device-vendor chain
  check; aaguid is logged), signCount is advisory unless
  `AUTH_WEBAUTHN_ENFORCE_SIGNCOUNT=true`, synced passkeys trust the vendor's
  sync boundary (TOTP remains the fully self-hosted fallback).
- **Enrollment QR** — the enroll page now renders the otpauth URI as a QR
  via the vendored qrcode-generator v1.4.4 (`internal/login/qrcode.min.js`,
  embedded + served at `/assets/qrcode.min.js` with an immutable cache
  header). Progressive enhancement: if the asset fails to load, the manual
  secret/URI (both select-all) remain. To bump the lib, replace the file,
  keep the MIT header, and run the `TestQRCodeAsset` + enroll-flow tests.
- **Single writer** — like every AOF service here, exactly one replica may
  write. Revisit if go-auth ever scales horizontally (the plan assumes one
  IdP instance).

# go-auth

Self-hosted OIDC identity provider: local users, argon2id passwords, TOTP 2FA
and passkeys (WebAuthn), serving RS256 JWTs that every k6n service verifies
through the shared `platform/auth` seam. It also holds a per-user secret vault
(encrypted at rest) whose **login** entries a companion browser extension
autofills and can import from Chrome.

Live at **https://users.k6n.net** (the permanent platform issuer). Replaces
Zitadel for first-party logins; Zitadel stays at `auth.k6n.net` for external
apps.

## Repository

This service lives in its own repo and is consumed by the
[`ecommerce` monorepo](https://git.k6n.net/mats/ecommerce) as a git submodule
at `go-auth/`. It no longer needs a monorepo checkout to build, test or
release.

```
cmd/auth/          composition root (env → AOF store → keys → OIDC provider)
internal/          oidc, users, webauthn, admin, mcp, reset, store, secrets, …
web/admin/         Vite + React admin SPA (built to dist/, served at runtime)
web/extension/     MV3 Chrome/Edge extension: vault autofill + Chrome import
agents.md          detailed service map — read this first
```

## Developing standalone

`go-auth` depends on one first-party module, `git.k6n.net/mats/platform`
(pinned in `go.mod`). It is private and sits behind no module proxy, so Go
needs to fetch it over SSH. One-time setup:

```bash
make setup                       # git config url."git@git.k6n.net:".insteadOf https://…
export GOPRIVATE=git.k6n.net     # add to your shell profile
```

Then the usual loop:

```bash
make test                        # go test ./...
make build                       # ./auth
make dev                         # build the admin UI + run on :8099
make ui-dev                      # Vite HMR, proxying the deployed issuer
```

> **Note:** because `platform` is a *published, versioned* dependency, a
> platform change reaches this repo only when its pin is bumped. The monorepo
> holds the platform source and publishes it (`make publish-platform` from the
> repo root, which pushes `platform/` to `git.k6n.net/mats/platform` and tags
> it). Keep the mint-side claims shape here in lockstep with the verifier in
> `platform/auth` — see `agents.md`.

## Local frontend development (device login + dev tokens)

`make ui-dev` runs the Vite dev server with a proxy to an auth service:
`AUTH_DEV_TARGET` picks which (`AUTH_DEV_TARGET=http://localhost:8099 make
ui-dev` for a local `make dev`); the default is the deployed issuer — the
intended way to work on a frontend is against the real thing. The proxy makes
the browser believe everything is same-origin, so cookies, WebAuthn
ceremonies and the JSON API all work without any CORS setup.

On `localhost` the proxied `/login` form still works, but a passkey cannot
(the WebAuthn RP ID is the issuer's host), and scripts and agents want a
token, not a cookie. The RFC 8628 device grant — the same one companion apps
use — is the bridge, reused end to end with **no new backend surface**:

- **In the browser:** dev builds of the console ship a small `dev auth`
  panel (bottom-right; an `import.meta.env.DEV`-gated chunk, so it never
  reaches the production bundle — `web/admin/src/dev/`). *Device login*
  starts a grant through the proxy and opens the issuer's `/device` page,
  where you approve with your account; the panel polls, then holds the
  access token as `Authorization: Bearer` on every `/api/*` call and keeps
  the rotating refresh token (a dev-only localStorage key) so `api()`
  renews silently when the ~15-minute access token expires. *Paste token*
  and *Copy token* cover the rest (`#token=…` deep links keep working).
- **In a terminal (humans and agents):** `scripts/dev-token.mjs` (node ≥ 18,
  no dependencies):

  ```bash
  node scripts/dev-token.mjs login    # prints the approval URL, waits, stores the refresh token
  node scripts/dev-token.mjs token    # prints a fresh access token (rotates the stored refresh token)
  node scripts/dev-token.mjs whoami   # GET /api/admin/me as that token
  GO_AUTH_TOKEN=… node scripts/dev-token.mjs token   # supply your own; nothing stored
  ```

  `AUTH_DEV_BASE` (or a positional argument) picks the issuer — default
  `https://users.k6n.net`; tokens live per host in `~/.go-auth/dev/`
  (mode 0600). Useful one-liner:

  ```bash
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(node scripts/dev-token.mjs token)" \
    https://users.k6n.net/api/admin/me
  ```

- **On the issuer:** a clientless device start (what both use) needs
  `AUTH_DEVICE_CLIENT_ID` to name the client such requests belong to. `make
  dev` sets it (`dev-console`); the cluster manifest ships it commented —
  uncomment it when pointing dev tooling at the live issuer. Without it the
  start request is refused with exactly that guidance, and a registered
  *public* client can be named explicitly instead
  (`scripts/dev-token.mjs --client-id …`). Approval is admin-gated, and the
  minted token carries the approver's identity and roles — the same contract
  a companion app gets.

## Password vault + browser extension

Every signed-in user has an encrypted secret vault (`/api/secrets`, owner-only:
the admin role unlocks nothing). Besides free-form secrets it stores **login**
entries — a site URL, a username and the password — so it doubles as a small
password manager.

`web/extension/` (Manifest V3, no build step) is the client: it fills login
forms from the vault and imports the passwords Chrome already saved
(`Settings → Passwords → Export`, a CSV). Sign-in is an ordinary
authorization-code + PKCE flow as a public OIDC client, so the extension needs
one registered client with a single redirect URI — the exact block to paste
into `AUTH_CLIENTS` is in [`web/extension/README.md`](web/extension/README.md).
The console's Account view can do the same import without the extension.
Matching is host-based (`internal/secrets/match.go`) and the browser only ever
sends the page origin; every password read is audited.

## WireGuard administration

If a [wireguard-helper](https://git.k6n.net/mats) instance is reachable, the
admin UI's **WireGuard** view lists its peers and can add/remove them, download
client configs, and re-import peers that were added to `wg0.conf` by hand.
go-auth does not run WireGuard and never touches `wg(8)` — it proxies to the
helper with an API key that stays server-side. The same operations are exposed
as MCP tools for agents.

Enable it with two env vars (both required; unset = the view shows "not
configured" and the service still starts):

```bash
AUTH_WIREGUARD_URL=http://10.10.1.2:8443   # the helper's listen address
AUTH_WIREGUARD_API_KEY=<helper API key>    # /etc/wireguard-helper/env on the helper
```

## Building and releasing

CI (`.gitea/workflows/build-push.yml`, Gitea Actions runner `amd64`) builds and
pushes `registry.k6n.net/ecommerce/auth:latest` on every push to `main` and
rolls the deployment out:

```bash
scripts/build-push.sh            # local equivalent; needs docker buildx + registry login
```

The Docker build takes `platform` as a BuildKit named context, fetched by the
script at the exact version pinned in `go.mod`, and points that requirement at
the context with a build-time `replace` — so the image build is hermetic and
needs no credentials or network inside the container. Kubernetes manifests
still live in the monorepo (`deploy/k8s/44-auth.yaml`) alongside the rest of
the cluster.

# ADR: capability-based tool policy and composed subagent authority

## Context
Subagents and worker tools required fine-grained sandboxing and capability enforcement to prevent unconstrained tool execution and unauthorized subagent authority escalation.

## Decision
Tool privileges are named by capabilities, not by tool identity: every ToolSpec/ToolDef carries required_capabilities (filesystem.read/write, process.exec, git.commit/push, scoped session.*/task.*/worker.* namespaces for built-ins, mcp.<category> stamped once per MCP server so policy outlives tool churn). Vocabulary in internal/domain/capabilities.go; pure evaluator in internal/capability. Most capabilities are baseline (held unless denied); a few are opt-in (harness.read, harness.write — no session holds them until granted), which is how the harness.* graph family is linked to behaviors instead of offered to everyone.

Grants/denies come from the selected skill (grant_capabilities:/deny_capabilities: front-matter in skills/*.md) or the built-in chat mode tables (mob grants the whole harness family; exploration only the read half), and are stamped durably on session events so replay never re-reads the skills directory. Enforcement is two-layer: the offer filter drops undeclared tools from every round's tool list, and dispatch re-checks the same declaration, failing with a durable CAPABILITY_DENIED naming the missing capability — including for worker-announced tools whose declarations live in the instance registry.

task.spawn composes child policy at spawn: kind (tool profile + round budget), read_only, lane, skill (same digest-pinned snapshot as an explicit selection), grant_capabilities, deny_capabilities. Two safety rules: the kind's profile ceiling is absolute (read-only kinds deny filesystem.write/git.commit/git.push by declaration — no request re-grants them), and every opt-in grant must be held by the parent — spawning subdivides authority, never widens it. Violations fail the spawn before any side effect. Worked example: skills/cms-content.md pairs an mcp.cms worker with denies that keep a content subagent out of repo files entirely.

## Consequences
Adding a tool means declaring capabilities honestly (the offer+dispatch double-check is the safety net); capability vocabulary changes are policy-relevant and should be additive; the durable CAPABILITY_DENIED events make denials auditable from the event stream alone.

# ADR: RabbitMQ broker topology — worker fanout, per-orchestrator result queues

## Context
Multiple workers and orchestrator instances need to coordinate dispatch and tool job completions safely without round-robining results to the wrong orchestrator or losing jobs on crash.

## Decision
Tool dispatch rides RabbitMQ (internal/adapters/rabbitmq). Tool jobs publish to the agent.tools topic exchange with routing key tool.<category>.<name>; every worker binds its own anonymous queue to tool.# and fulfills the jobs it owns by name/category (ownership by registration), ignoring the rest. Instance/repo targeting rides job headers (InstanceID pinned via session extra.worker / longest-prefix extra.repo match).

Results and started-pings publish on the results/started keys; each orchestrator instance consumes its own DURABLE queue agent.tools.results.<id> / agent.tools.started.<id> (id = ORCHESTRATOR_INSTANCE_ID, default hostname). Because every orchestrator on a shared broker receives every result, the handlers are idempotent: only the instance that owns the session's event store applies a completion; the rest no-op. This is what makes a second orchestrator (e.g. local compose pointed at the same cluster broker) safe — a shared named queue would round-robin results to a random orchestrator and stall sessions.

## Consequences
ORCHESTRATOR_INSTANCE_ID must stay stable per deployment (compose dev, k8s prod) so durable queues survive restarts and drain what was published while down. A permanently decommissioned instance keeps receiving every result into its queues — routing follows the exchange binding, not session ownership — so it must have agent.tools.results.<id> and agent.tools.started.<id> deleted (rabbitmqctl), and a stopped-but-temporary instance should be restarted or its queues purged before they grow. DLX/DLQ (agent.tools.dlx / agent.tools.dlq) and a retry queue exist for poison jobs.

# ADR: streamproc is the single read seam; projections are disposable

## Context
Direct reading and re-reading of raw stream files from multiple components created read coupling, race conditions, and out-of-order session states across instances.

## Decision
All live reads go through internal/streamproc, fed by the event store's append bus (SubscribeAppend) — nothing re-reads stream files to stay current. SessionView (per-session event slice + lazy domain.Fold) implements ports.SessionReader and is the only sanctioned source of live session state; ToolLedger is the tool dispatch ledger (replaced coord.json, one apply path shared by bus and boot replay); ToolRoundView derives tool-round settlement per iteration with an in-memory Wait (no polling). Tailing projections (instances, sessions, memory, compaction, digest in internal/adapters/projection/memory) run as streamproc.Runner goroutines with global-position checkpoints; snapshots mirror to <AOL dir>/projections/ via temp+rename write-behind and are disposable by design — losing one only costs a replay; a stale snapshot falls back to a one-time full replay after head validation.

The ONE exception: internal/orchestrator/replay.go (FoldAt) reads session streams directly from the store for time-travel (promptAt, contextReplay). SessionsView derives rows from SessionView folds (no state machine of its own). Engine wiring order matters: Attach subscribes SessionView+ToolLedger BEFORE restoring so mid-restore batches dedupe by position; a Runner built any other way never sees live appends.

## Consequences
Adding a read model = write a Runner + fold, never a new file reader; debugging starts from the event table (the source of truth) and the Context Replay endpoints (/api/sessions/:id/context?budgets=,prune=1) rather than ad-hoc greps; boot cost scales with store size (delta replay with anchor validation mitigates).

# ADR: Event-sourced core, single writer, canonical pointer events

## Context
Previous architecture experienced an NFS corruption incident (2026-09-06) when multiple writers truncated streams to their own cursors. The orchestrator must guarantee write integrity and crash recovery over distributed filesystems.

## Decision
The system of record is an append-only event store (AOL: one stream file per session under AOL_DIR). Appends are OCC (expected version), fsync-optional (AOL_FSYNC/AOL_FLUSH_MS). The orchestrator is the SINGLE WRITER of the store dir: a second batched writer truncates stream files back to its own cursor — this caused the NFS corruption incident of 2026-09-06, so compaction, RAG memory sync, and digest all run as in-process projections appending through the one writer, and the k8s deployment uses Recreate strategy on a singleton with a 5Gi PVC. OpenCoord claims a file lock (claimWriterLock) to enforce this at runtime.

Events are canonical pointer types: Store.Append normalizes via domain.Canonical (internal/domain/registry.go), so the append bus, stream files, and Load all deliver exactly one Go type per event; consumers type-switch on pointers only. Event types are versioned (user_message_received.v1, tool_call_requested.v1, session_compacted.v1, worker_instance_announced.v1, …); unknown types on load are tolerated (forward compatibility). Torn-tail and zero-filled-line recovery is implemented and tested (corruption_test.go).

## Consequences
Every durable side effect must be expressed as an event appended through the single writer; direct file reads of streams are forbidden except time-travel replay (orchestrator/replay.go). Message pump crash recovery rides the same machinery (durable drive queue + leases in drive.go/drive_mem.go: a session left THINKING by a dead driver is resumed with its interrupted round completed once the lease lapses). Availability of the orchestrator is sacrificed for write integrity — mitigated by durable broker queues and drive-lease recovery on restart.

# eventsourced-ai Architecture Overview

## Context
Hexagonal architecture for autonomous multi-agent systems requiring deterministic event replay, high write integrity across distributed filesystems, and strict security isolation.

## Decision
eventsourced-ai is structured around an event-sourced core with a single-writer append-only event store, streamproc as the unified read seam, RabbitMQ topic exchange topology for worker dispatch, and capability-based policy enforcement across all tools and spawned subagents.

## Consequences
Guarantees full auditability and crash recovery across restarts while isolating subagent capabilities and maintaining bounded context windows via compaction.

## Topology
Binaries under cmd/: orchestrator, worker-code, worker-tools, worker-mcp, worker-browser, and web/ dashboard.

## Domain Core
Hexagonal domain boundaries: append-only-log file store, versioned canonical pointer events, and pure session folding.

## Streamproc Read Seam
internal/streamproc is the single read seam feeding SessionView, ToolLedger, and disposable projections.

## Context Management Pipeline
Per-round context caps, deterministic pruning, and LLM compaction guarding a 90% window limit.

## Messaging
RabbitMQ agent.tools topic exchange with worker fanout and per-orchestrator durable result queues.

## Capability Model
Tool privileges governed by capability declarations with offer-filter and dispatch-verification double checks.

## Deployment
Homelab k8s dev namespace: orchestrator Recreate deployment with 5Gi PVC and managed workers.
